l2:l2.seq.no-refresh.01.source: textbook SRAM (GENERIC); the idle rail: docs/energy-manual/04a-fine-grain.md:110 and its table (67 °C 1.698 W, 82 °C 2.726 W)
l2:l2.seq.no-refresh.01.note: Applies only if the arrays are SRAM (l2.storage-question).

l2:l2.seq.no-refresh.02.statement: no scrub, no sleep in service: ET-SoC-1 has no background ECC scrub (a reserved bit, 'implemented in Gepardo'). Deep sleep and shut-down are only for non-operational shires, and the cards show no wake-up latency after idle. The only whole-array sweep is the power-up Idx_All_Inv of the tag-state RAM.
l2:l2.seq.no-refresh.02.source: external/core-et/docs/CORE-ET-Shire-Cache-Specification.pdf (v1.1), pdf p.99, pdf p.101, pdf p.88-89; docs/findings/16-dvfs-and-leakage.md:123

l2:l2.u-zero-partial.statement: Whether a partial write that leaves a line all zero sets the tag state's zero bit (a fill or a full-line write does, in the re-implementation RTL).
l2:l2.u-zero-partial.source: none: external/core-et/docs/CORE-ET-Shire-Cache-Specification.pdf pdf p.47 Table 12, p.101 do not say; shirecache_bank_mesh.sv:346 covers whole lines only

l3:l3.what.statement: The L3 is memory-side and distributed: each of the 32 compute shires gives a 1 MB slice of its 4 MB shire cache to a chip-wide L3 of 32 MB. The datasheet calls all 140 MB of on-die storage SRAM, each 1 MB block usable as L2, a slice of the L3, or scratchpad.
l3:l3.what.source: external/et-man/ET Preliminary Datasheet Rev 1.0.pdf pdf p.4 §1 (external/et-man/txt/ET Preliminary Datasheet Rev 1.0.txt:96-98) and pdf p.13 §2.1.3.1 (txt:564-571); docs/reports/data/2026-09-22-cards/driver_config.json `l3_kb` 32768 on every card

l3:l3.homes.statement: Only the 32 compute shires are homes of the chip-wide L3: the home field is 5 bits (PA[10:6]) for a 32-shire configuration, so no line of the 32 MB L3 lives in the master, spare, PCIe or I/O shire (the I/O shire's own L2/L3 cache serves its Maxions).
l3:l3.homes.source: external/core-et/docs/CORE-ET-Shire-Cache-Specification.pdf pdf p.26 §1.4.2.3 ('For a 32-Shire SoC, there are five ShireID bits ... bits [10:6]'); external/core-et-main/hw/ip/shirecache/rtl/shirecache_pkg.sv:142-143 (L3Shires 32)

l3:l3.partition-m0.statement: The cards run cache mode M0: in every sub-bank, RAM sets 0-639 are scratchpad, 640-767 L2 and 768-1023 (base 0x300, 256 sets, set mask 0xFF) the L3. The chip comes out of reset in M0 and the firmware computes the L3 base as scratchpad size + L2 size.
l3:l3.partition-m0.source: external/core-et/docs/CORE-ET-Shire-Cache-Specification.pdf pdf p.21-22 Tables 6-7 ('The chip will come out of reset in mode M0'); external/core-et/rtl/shire/esr/esr_cache_bank.v:104-113 (reset defaults: L3 base 24/32, size 8/32 of the sets for a 4 MB build); external/et-platform/device-bootloaders/src/ServiceProcessorBL2/driver/bl2_cache_control.c:712-721; docs/reports/data/2026-09-22-cards/driver_config.json (l2_kb 16384, l3_kb 32768, scp_kb 81920: M0)

l3:l3.slice-arith.statement: One slice = 4 banks x 4 sub-banks x 256 sets x 4 ways x 64 B = 1 MB (16,384 lines per shire, 4,096 per bank).
l3:l3.slice-arith.source: arithmetic on external/core-et/docs/CORE-ET-Shire-Cache-Specification.pdf pdf p.20 Table 4 and pdf p.22 Table 7 (M0 L3: 256 sets per sub-bank)

l3:l3.same-arrays.statement: The L3 is not a separate memory. It is the top quarter of the same arrays that hold the L2 and the scratchpad: in each data macro (4,096 words) the L3 lines are words 3,072-4,095 (address {set 768-1023, way}); in each tag and tag-state macro (1,024 rows) rows 768-1023. Per shire that is a quarter of 64 data, 16 tag and 16 tag-state macros.
l3:l3.same-arrays.source: external/core-et/docs/CORE-ET-Shire-Cache-Specification.pdf pdf p.22 Table 7 (L3 base 0x300, end 0x3FF), pdf p.51 (macro sizes); external/core-et-main/hw/ip/shirecache/rtl/shirecache_pipe_sub_bank.sv:1613 (data RAM address = {pipe_set, tag_ram_hit_way}); external/core-et-main/hw/ip/shirecache/rtl/shirecache_pipe.sv:1010 (one tag, tag-state and data RAM wrapper per sub-bank); external/core-et-main/hw/ip/shirecache/rtl/shirecache_pipe_data_ram_wrap.sv:83-107 (four quadword RAMs)
l3:l3.same-arrays.note: Macro counts: 4 banks x 4 sub-banks x (1 tag + 1 tag-state + 4 data). The I-cache macro (mbi) and the dataq (mbq) are separate.

l3:l3.decode.statement: L3 address decode (default swizzle0): offset PA[5:0], home shire PA[10:6], bank PA[12:11], sub-bank PA[14:13], set from PA[15] up (PA[22:15] for M0's 256 sets), 23-bit tag stored from PA[17] up. Consecutive 64 B lines rotate over the 32 homes; lines 2 KB apart change bank, 8 KB apart sub-bank.
l3:l3.decode.source: external/core-et/docs/CORE-ET-Shire-Cache-Specification.pdf pdf p.24 §1.4.1.2 and pdf p.27 Table 8 (swizzle0); external/core-et-main/hw/ip/shirecache/rtl/shirecache_pkg.sv:104-112; external/core-et/rtl/shire/esr/esr_cache_bank.v:84-103 (swizzle reset = mode 0); docs/research/counters-and-dram.md:373-377 (sc_l3_shire_swizzle_ctl left at reset)

l3:l3.home-measured.statement: The home-by-PA[10:6] rule holds on silicon: 1,498 of 1,500 random lines timed from shire 0 fall within 4 cycles of 110 + 12 x hops(requester, PA[10:6]) (aifoundry2, 19 Sep), and 99.4-99.97% of lines on each of three cards (26 Sep).

l3:l3.alias.statement: Default two-shire aliasing: the tag stores PA[10] (the home ID's top bit) in its lowest bit, so a dead shire's L3 lines can be redirected to the shire 16 IDs away and still be told apart. All-shire aliasing stores PA[10:6]; the firmware sets it only when reconfiguring the NoC for 8 or fewer shires.

l3:l3.geometry.statement: Every sub-bank holds a tag RAM of 1,024 x 116 bits (4 ways x (23-bit tag + 6 ECC bits)), a tag-state RAM of 1,024 x 40 (4 ways x {valid, locked, zero, qwen[3:0]} + 5-bit LRU code + 7 ECC bits) and four data RAMs of 4,096 x 144 (128 data + 16 ECC bits: 8 per 64-bit doubleword). 4-way set-associative, 64 B lines, write-back, write-allocate, LRU.
l3:l3.geometry.source: external/core-et/docs/CORE-ET-Shire-Cache-Specification.pdf pdf p.8-9 §1.1, pdf p.47 §2.14.2-2.14.3 (Table 12), pdf p.48-49 §2.14.5-2.14.6.2, pdf p.51; external/core-et-main/hw/ip/shirecache/rtl/shirecache_pkg.sv:61-79
l3:l3.geometry.note: The spec's feature list (pdf p.9) says 7 ECC bits per 33-bit tag and 6 per 33 bits of state; its storage chapter (pdf p.47-49) and the macro widths 116 and 40 say 6 per 23-bit tag and 7 per 33 bits of state. The macro widths decide it.

l3:l3.macros.statement: The cache RAMs are compiled macros bought from a third party: tag-state mbs = saculs0g4l2p1024x40m4b1w0c0p0d0s1rm0rw11 (type '2PUHDRF'; the spec says the state RAM is two-ported), tag mbt = saduls0g4l1p1024x116m4b1w0c0p0d0s1rm0sdrw11 and data mbd = saduls0g4l1p4096x144m4b4w0c0p0d0s1rm0sdrw11 (type '1PUHD'). The spec calls the data array 'SRAM memory panels'.
l3:l3.macros.source: external/core-et/docs/CORE-ET-Shire-Cache-Specification.pdf pdf p.48 §2.14.5 ('SRAM memory panels that are 144 bits wide') and §2.14.6.1 ('Intellectual Property (IP) acquired from a third party vendor'), pdf p.51 §2.14.6.4, pdf p.45 ('the state RAM is two-ported')
l3:l3.macros.note: Reading '1PUHD' as single-port ultra-high-density and 'm4'/'b4' as column mux 4 and 4 internal banks follows common memory-compiler naming; no source in the drop states it (see u.macro-geometry).

l3:l3.vendor.statement: The macros' vendor is not named. Three hints point to Synopsys-compiled memories: Ainekko's translation guide lists 'Synopsys ASIC SRAMs (saduls0g4l1p*, etc.)', the spec's BIST is 'a shared bus BIST, such as the Synopsys SMS', and the BIST wrappers in the open build script are named sms_sram_wr_<macro>. That the memories are Synopsys's is an inference, as at the L2.
l3:l3.vendor.note: AGENTS.md is a guide for translating the RTL, written in 2026, not a tape-out record. The gen_bist_br wrappers are the I/O shire's (its shire cache uses the same 4096x144 data-macro size); the minion shire's are not listed there. 'Synopsys' for the vendor rests on these three sources, none of them a purchase record.

l3:l3.trim-table.statement: Each macro has trim bits: read margin RM[3:0] (with enable RME), read assist RA[1:0], write assist WA[2:0] and write pulse WPULSE[2:0], set per logical RAM by ESR. For the tag and data macros (1PUHD) the spec's rows are RM mode 0: Vmin 585 mV, Vnom 650, WA 7, RA 1; RM1: 630/700, WA 7, RA 1; RM2: 650/722, WA 6, RA 0; up to RM5: 855/950. The default is RM0 'to allow nominal 650mV operation'.

l3:l3.trim-reset.statement: The emulator's reset values of shire_cache_ram_cfg1 (0xE800340) and cfg2 (0x03A0) decode to RME 0, RM 0, RA 1, WA 7, WPULSE 0 for the tag and data macros and RA 2, WA 6 for the tag-state macros: exactly the spec's RM0 rows. No firmware in the drop writes these registers.
l3:l3.trim-reset.source: external/et-platform/sw-sysemu/esrs_et.cpp:46-47 decoded with etsoc_shire_other_esr.h:3073-3364; grep of external/et-platform/device-bootloaders finds no write to SHIRE_CACHE_RAM_CFG*
l3:l3.trim-reset.note: The HAL header gives these fields no reset value (RESET_MASK 0xfffffff000000000 for cfg1), so what the silicon holds is not established: u.live-settings.

l3:l3.sram-rail.statement: The SRAM rail sits at 705 mV (703-707 mV on the die at idle, per shire), well above the minion rail (517-521 mV) and the mesh rail (483-486 mV).

l3:l3.rail-vs-trim.statement: At 705 mV the tag and data macros run between the spec's RM1 row (Vnom 700 mV) and RM2 row (722 mV), 55 mV above the RM0 row's 650 mV nominal that the reset trim selects.
l3:l3.rail-vs-trim.note: Whether RM0 or a higher row is programmed on these cards is u.live-settings.

l3:l3.hv-region.statement: The Shire Channel, which holds the shire cache, the UC block and the I-cache data memory, is a high-voltage region: the I-cache memory sits there 'because it has to be operated at high voltage'. The mesh routers sit on their own low-voltage rail, and the router side of each crossing is low voltage.
l3:l3.hv-region.source: external/core-et/docs/CORE-ET Minion Shire Description.pdf pdf p.10 §3.1 and pdf p.18 §5; external/core-et/rtl/libs/mems_and_fifos/vcfifo_nsip_brdg2rtr.v:9 (via docs/reports/data/2026-09-24-wire-energy/research/SYNTHESIS.md:74)
l3:l3.hv-region.note: Which rail feeds the shire-cache logic (the SRAM rail or another) is in the Power Spec, which is not in the drop: u.rail-of-logic.

l3:l3.clock.statement: The shire cache runs on shire_clock, the same clock as the minions (the neighbourhood clock is shire_clock shifted 180 degrees; the errata: every area of a minion shire except the NoC uses the same clock), so 600 MHz on these cards; the mesh runs on clk__noc, 400 MHz.
l3:l3.clock.source: external/core-et/docs/CORE-ET Minion Shire Description.pdf pdf p.12 Table 2; external/et-man/ET-SoC Errata.pdf pdf p.42; clk__noc 400 MHz: telemetry mhz.noc (docs/reports/data/2026-09-20-power-aifoundry2/horace-telemetry.jsonl) and SYNTHESIS.md:72

l3:l3.clock-gating.statement: Each data macro's clock is gated: an integrated clock gate (latch + AND) opens only while the pipeline accesses that sub-bank and for ram_delay cycles after; the spec asks that address and write-enable inputs stay unchanged when a RAM is not accessed.
l3:l3.clock-gating.source: external/core-et-main/hw/ip/shirecache/rtl/shirecache_pipe_data_ram_wrap.sv:52-72; external/core-et-main/AGENTS.md:100 (prim_clk_gate: 'latch + AND (ASIC ICG pattern)'); external/core-et/docs/CORE-ET-Shire-Cache-Specification.pdf pdf p.46 §2.14.1.5, §2.14.1.11

l3:l3.panels.statement: A read enables all four 144-bit data panels of the sub-bank; a write enables only the panels whose quadword enable is set ('a Partial Write that just changes three words does not need to activate more than three memory panels').

l3:l3.zero-state.statement: Zero lines skip the data array. When a fill or a full-line write brings an all-zero line (the bank computes the NOR of all 512 bits as the line arrives), the tag state's zero bit is set and the data macros are not written; a later read of that line does not read them either and returns zeros. Enabled by default (esr_sc_zero_state_enable = 1).
l3:l3.zero-state.source: external/core-et/docs/CORE-ET-Shire-Cache-Specification.pdf pdf p.47 Table 12 ('zero ... cache memory must not be read') and pdf p.101 (esr_sc_zero_state_enable); external/core-et-main/hw/ip/shirecache/rtl/shirecache_bank_mesh.sv:346 (zero_data = ~|data); external/core-et-main/hw/ip/shirecache/rtl/shirecache_pipe_sub_bank.sv:810 (no data RAM read on a zero hit), 983-1001, 1051-1063 (no data RAM write)
l3:l3.zero-state.note: The zeros still cross the mesh as 512 data bits. Whether the cards run with the feature on is u.live-settings.

l3:l3.no-refresh.statement: The shire-cache specification describes no refresh or retention circuit for its RAMs, only deep_sleep (a low-leakage retention mode) and shut_down (data lost) for the RAMs of shires that are not operational.
l3:l3.no-refresh.note: A text search of the spec for 'refresh' finds nothing.

l3:l3.ecc-scrub.statement: A single-bit ECC error is corrected in the pipeline's ECC stages (te for tags, de for data) but not written back: the scrub pass is a reserved bit, for future chips.
l3:l3.ecc-scrub.source: external/core-et/docs/CORE-ET-Shire-Cache-Specification.pdf pdf p.46 §2.14.1.8, §2.14.1.14; pdf p.99 (esr_sc_ecc_scrub_enable: 'Future chips will implement this feature')

l3:l3.ports.statement: Each shire meets the mesh with 4 L3-slave ports (incoming L3 and remote-scratchpad requests, 512 bits, one request per cycle each), 4 to_l3 master ports and 1 to_sys master port (to memory). AXI channels cross into the NoC through voltage-changing FIFOs with 2-stage synchronizers.
l3:l3.ports.source: external/core-et/docs/CORE-ET-Shire-Cache-Specification.pdf pdf p.8, pdf p.11 (VCFIFO, 2-stage synchronizers), pdf p.32-34 §2.3-2.4 ('four for the L3 mesh and one for the SYS mesh'); external/core-et-main/hw/ip/shirecache/rtl/shirecache_pkg.sv:138-139

l3:l3.lane.statement: Which of the 4 lanes an L3 request takes is set by the bank it will use at the home, PA[12:11] under swizzle0, not by PA[7:6]; PA[7:6] picks the lane only for remote-scratchpad requests. At the home the request goes to bank PA[12:11].
l3:l3.lane.source: external/core-et-main/hw/ip/shirecache/rtl/shirecache_mesh_master.sv:132-153 (req_bank_id = remote SCP ? PA[7:6] : L3 bank from shirecache_pipe_l3_swizzle_get); external/core-et/docs/CORE-ET-Shire-Cache-Specification.pdf pdf p.100 (the swizzle fields are used 'by the incoming L3 distribute design to select the correct bank')
l3:l3.lane.note: The lane rule rests on core-et-main alone, Ainekko's co-simulated translation of the CORE-ET RTL; spec p.100 says only that the swizzle picks the bank at the incoming L3 side. Heat per millimetre's lane rule (PA[7:6], chip fact L103) is right for its remote-scratchpad flows; for L3 lines the lane is the home bank (to confirm).

l3:l3.reqq.statement: Each bank has a 64-entry request queue, up to 21 entries of it reserved for L3-slave requests; two entries can be allocated per cycle, one for a neighbourhood request and one for an L3 request.
l3:l3.reqq.page: One hot line stops a shire

l3:l3.priority.statement: L3-slave requests win over the shire's own requests for a sub-bank (the second of three arbitration steps) unless esr_sc_l3_yield_priority_cnt is set; two errata record neighbourhood requests starved or hung behind L3-slave traffic.
l3:l3.priority.source: external/core-et/docs/CORE-ET-Shire-Cache-Specification.pdf pdf p.36 §2.6 (Figure 8), pdf p.99; external/et-man/ET-SoC Errata.pdf pdf p.80-81 (§4.1, §4.2)
l3:l3.priority.page: One hot line stops a shire

l3:l3.pipeline.statement: A read goes down the bank's non-stalling pipeline in two phases, tag then data: ag, ad (allocate), rqa (arbitrate), tap, ta, ta0, ta1 (tag and tag-state RAM access), te (tag ECC), tc (tag compare: hit, miss, victim), then dap, da, da0, da1 (data RAM access), de (data ECC), dc (data complete, OR'd from the sub-banks to the response mux).

l3:l3.hit-way-read.statement: Only the hit way is read: the data RAM address {set, hit way} is formed after the tag compare, so one 144-bit word per panel is read, not the four ways' data.
l3:l3.hit-way-read.source: external/core-et-main/hw/ip/shirecache/rtl/shirecache_pipe_sub_bank.sv:1613; external/core-et/docs/CORE-ET-Shire-Cache-Specification.pdf pdf p.44 (pipeline diagram: data read after tag compare)

l3:l3.ram-delay.statement: RAM access takes 2 cycles by default (esr_sc_ram_delay = 2; 3 or 4 possible), so a sub-bank accepts a request every 2 cycles and a bank one per cycle across its 4 sub-banks; a fill that evicts a victim (read then write) holds a sub-bank for 4 cycles.
l3:l3.ram-delay.source: external/core-et/docs/CORE-ET-Shire-Cache-Specification.pdf pdf p.36 (busy rule 1), pdf p.44-45, pdf p.101; external/core-et/rtl/inc/shire_cache_defines.vh:260 (SC_RAM_DELAY_DEFAULT 2)
l3:l3.ram-delay.note: No firmware in the drop writes sc_pipe_ctl; the live value is u.live-settings.

l3:l3.mru-write.statement: An L3 read hit also writes: the LRU code is updated (the hit way becomes most recent) through the tag-state RAM's second port, which lets one pass read and write it.
l3:l3.mru-write.source: external/core-et-main/hw/ip/shirecache/rtl/shirecache_pipe_sub_bank.sv:843-859 (update_mru_tc includes L3Read hits), 884-888; external/core-et/docs/CORE-ET-Shire-Cache-Specification.pdf pdf p.45 ('the state RAM is two-ported'), pdf p.47-48 §2.14.4

l3:l3.no-rbuf.statement: L3 reads never use the bank's 8-entry read buffer, so every L3 hit reads the tag, tag-state and data macros (L2 and scratchpad reads can be served from the buffer).
l3:l3.no-rbuf.source: external/core-et/docs/CORE-ET-Shire-Cache-Specification.pdf pdf p.11 Table 1 ('L3 does not access the Read buffer'), pdf p.40 §2.8

l3:l3.spec-latency.statement: Designed idle latencies in shire clocks, crossbars included: L3 read hit 30 (from the L3-slave AXI read request to its response), L3 read miss 42 + NoC and memory, and at the requester an L2 read miss 34 + NoC and L3.

l3:l3.partial.statement: The L3, unlike the L2, can hold partial lines left by write-arounds; a read that hits one first evicts the partial line to memory and reads it back.

l3:l3.write.statement: L3 writes carry full lines, quadword enables or partials: a write that misses is installed with dirty bits for its quadwords (no fill for whole quadwords); one that hits a clean line marks all four quadwords dirty.

l3:l3.writearound.statement: Tensor stores reach the L3 as write-arounds: they coalesce in the requesting shire's L2 buffer (32 entries per bank) and go to the home when all four 16-byte quadwords of the line are written, or on a flush or eviction.

l3:l3.miss-path.statement: An L3 miss leaves the home through its to_sys port to the memory shire PA[8:6]; the data returns as an L3 fill (which may evict a victim, written back over to_sys if dirty) and the home answers the requester.
l3:l3.miss-path.source: external/core-et/docs/CORE-ET-Shire-Cache-Specification.pdf pdf p.55 §3.2.2 ('Misses and victims are directed to the to_sys mesh port'), Figure 14; docs/research/counters-and-dram.md:478-482

l3:l3.dram-leg.statement: Past the L3 a DRAM load adds 91 + 12 cycles per hop from the home to the memory shire (the constant 90-91 on three cards).

l3:l3.lat-fit.statement: L3 hit, load to use: 110.5 + 11.99 cycles per mesh hop between the requester and the home shire, on each of three cards (5 passes each); within 4 cycles for 99.4-99.97% of lines.

l3:l3.lat-by-home.statement: From shire 0 (aifoundry2, 19 Sep, median of each home's lines): 109 cycles when the home is shire 0 itself, 121-122 at 1 hop, 133-134 at 2, 157-158 at 4, 181-182 at 6, 218 at 9 hops.

l3:l3.lat-by-requester.statement: Averaged over all 32 homes (pointer chase over a 4 MB working set): 168.8-168.9 cycles from shires 0 and 31, 160.6-160.7 from shire 7, 159.1-159.2 from shire 24, in every pass on three cards.

l3:l3.lat-clock-split.statement: Chases at 600 and 800 MHz split the L3 constant: 72.2 cycles scale with the core clock and 61.4 ns do not, plus 20 ns per mesh hop (72.2 cycles + 61.4 ns = 109 cycles at 600 MHz).
l3:l3.lat-clock-split.unit: ns not scaling with the core clock

l3:l3.lat-reconcile.statement: The spec's counts do not add up to the measured split: an L2 miss (34 shire clocks) plus an L3 hit at the home (30) is 64 clock-scaled cycles, and the L1 and neighbourhood path adds about 26 more (L2 hit 47 measured against 21 in the spec), about 90 against the 72.2 measured. The anatomy page's split of the 110 (about 48 to miss the L1 and L2, about 62 for the home slice) is an estimate.
l3:l3.lat-reconcile.source: external/core-et/docs/CORE-ET-Shire-Cache-Specification.pdf pdf p.11 Table 1; docs/findings/05-claims.md:379, 421 (L2 hit 47); docs/research/counters-and-dram.md:476; workloads/memprobe/report_template.html:880-881
l3:l3.lat-reconcile.note: Where the 61 ns go (four voltage-and-clock crossings, the NoC bridges, the mesh stops at 0 hops) is u.latency-split.

l3:l3.hop.statement: Each mesh hop adds 12 cycles to the round trip at 600 MHz: 20 ns, which is 16 cycles at 800 MHz. The same 12.00 per hop holds for L3 hits (11.99), remote scratchpad (12.00) and TensorSend (12.02).

l3:l3.hop-noc-cycles.statement: 20 ns per hop round trip is 10 ns, or 4 cycles of the 400 MHz NoC clock, per hop each way, if request and reply take equal time.
l3:l3.hop-noc-cycles.unit: NoC cycles per hop each way
l3:l3.hop-noc-cycles.note: A published measurement (Chang) reports 3 cycles per direction at an unstated clock; not reconciled.

l3:l3.tsend-compare.statement: For comparison, a 32 B TensorSend round trip between two shires is 150 + 12.02 cycles per hop: the same 12 per hop as an L3 hit but a larger fixed cost (register to register through both shires' message paths) than the L3's 110.

l3:l3.mean-hops.statement: On the measured map a requester is on average 3.75 hops from a line's home (all 32 x 32 pairs, self included): 2.81 from the best-placed shire, 5.00 from corner shires 0 and 31, 10 at most. By the fit an average L3 hit costs about 155 cycles (258 ns) chip-wide, 144-170 by requester, and 230 cycles (383 ns) at 10 hops.
l3:l3.mean-hops.source: computed here from workloads/nocbench/analyze.py:52-60 (MARTY) and l3.lat-fit
l3:l3.mean-hops.note: The fit predicts 170.5, 162.2, 160.7 and 170.5 cycles for requesters 0, 7, 24 and 31, 1-2 cycles above l3.lat-by-requester's chases.

l3:l3.route.statement: Routes are minimal (latency is linear in Manhattan distance over all 496 pairs, through the four non-compute cells too); and in dimension order: a request goes x first, then y, and its reply y first, then x, back along the request's links (measured on aifoundry1 card 1, aifoundry3 and aifoundry2 on 29 September, E56; chip:L104). Which of the nine router layers L3 traffic uses and how wide a link is are not documented in the drop.
l3:l3.route.source: docs/findings/05-claims.md:392; docs/reports/data/2026-09-24-wire-energy/research/SYNTHESIS.md:66-68, 75; the order: docs/reports/data/2026-09-29-nocr (E56), the chip tour's fact L104
l3:l3.route.note: Until 29 September the order was not known and this page drew every route x first. E56 streamed tensor loads and stores between compute shires' scratchpads; that an L3 home's and a memory shire's replies take the same order is inferred.

l3:l3.flits.statement: A read request is about 75-85 bits (AXI AR); the reply is one 512-bit data beat plus RID/RRESP/RLAST (524-534 bits) and a NetSpeed header of unknown width. Only the reply carries the line.

l3:l3.mesh-rail.statement: The mesh (routers, links, NetSpeed bridges) runs at 485 mV set (484 at the die) and 400 MHz on these cards.

l3:l3.bw.statement: Every minion streaming from the L3: 0.98 TB/s chip-wide at 600 MHz, 1.6 B per minion-cycle, about 30.7 GB/s per slice; the own L2 gives 2.45 TB/s.

l3:l3.bw-tload.statement: Tensor loads by all 1,024 minions (32 KB touched per hart, stride 8 KB, so the set fits the L3) read the L3 at 1,072 GB/s on all three cards.

l3:l3.energy.statement: An L3 byte costs 14.7 pJ above idle [7.1-20.5 over 18 passes] (1 KB tensor loads by every minion, 768 KB per shire, 600 MHz): aifoundry2 12.3, aifoundry3 13.5, aifoundry1 card 1 18.4 pJ/B; 4.7x an L2 byte (3.11), about an eighth of a DRAM byte (114.6). About 0.94 nJ per 64 B line.
l3:l3.energy.note: The probe did not set the L3's contents (04-bytes-memory.md:21).

l3:l3.energy-contents.statement: With the contents set, L3 reads cost 2.5x more on random data than on zeros: 7.6 vs 19.3 pJ/B on aifoundry2, 7.5 vs 18.8 on aifoundry3, 9.0 vs 22.8 on aifoundry1 card 1 (tensor loads at 1,072 GB/s).

l3:l3.energy-rails.statement: Split by rail (aifoundry2, same runs): random data 7.5 pJ/B on the SRAM rail, 7.5 on the mesh rail, 1.4 on the minion rail (20.6 W over idle in all); zeros 2.9, 3.2 and 0.6 pJ/B (8.1 W). The SRAM rail falls 2.6x on zeros, the mesh rail 2.3x.
l3:l3.energy-rails.note: aifoundry3: SRAM 7.92 / 3.15 W, mesh 7.87 / 3.39 W; aifoundry1-c1: SRAM 6.84 / 2.76 W, mesh 9.39 / 4.06 W. A zero line skips the data macros at both ends (l3.zero-state), which fits a large SRAM-rail drop; the share is u.zero-share.

l3:l3.energy-per-load.statement: Per 64 B line read from the L3 by 1 KB tensor loads through the mesh (a working set whose lines are homed across the chip), on random data: 1,233, 1,203 and 1,461 pJ above idle (19.3, 18.8 and 22.8 pJ/B), of which 39, 39 and 28% on the SRAM rail (the L2 miss, the L3 read and the L2 fill), 39% on the mesh rail, 7, 6 and 7% on the minion rail and 14, 16 and 27% on no metered rail (aifoundry2, aifoundry3 and aifoundry1 card 1). Each mesh hop adds 115 pJ per line on random data and 43 on zeros (1.80 and 0.67 pJ/B, the mean of the energy manual's straight lines through another shire's scratchpad at 1-8 hops).
l3:l3.energy-per-load.unit: % on the SRAM rail (L3 read through the mesh, aifoundry2)
l3:l3.energy-per-load.source: docs/reports/data/2026-09-23-energy-manual/manual.json catalogue.cards.<card>.summary['dramrow/stride8K/random'] (rails_over_w, over_idle_w, pj_per_byte) and catalogue.cards.<card>.wire.<zeros|random>.slope_pj_per_byte_per_hop, as Anatomy of a memory access §6 gives them (workloads/memprobe/build_report.py)
l3:l3.energy-per-load.note: Until 28 September this row gave the first measurement, on 19 September on aifoundry2 alone (one 8-byte ld per line, a local or a far home; docs/reports/data/2026-09-19-memprobe-aifoundry2/summary.json power.l3near, .l3far); Anatomy of a memory access keeps those runs as one note, and its §6 shows this split.

l3:l3.wire-energy.statement: A random bit costs 36.2 fJ per mm on the mesh rail over free links (46.7 on board power). A 64 B reply over one 3.72 mm hop is then about 69 pJ on the mesh rail (1.1 pJ/B per hop); on board power a hop measures 115 pJ per line on random data and 43 on zeros (l3.energy-per-load).
l3:l3.wire-energy.note: The per-hop product (512 bits x 36.2 fJ x 3.72 mm) is computed here and ignores the request and headers.

l3:l3.gather.statement: A gather that goes straight to the home slice (fgwg.ps, random lines, 4 KB per hart) costs 1.53 nJ per 4-byte element at 6.46 G elements/s: each element fetches its own 64 B line, about 24 pJ per line byte.

l3:l3.atomic.statement: Global atomics execute in the home bank's atomic block: one contended line retires an atomic every 10.00 cycles (about 60 M/s for the chip); an uncontended remote global atomic takes 216 cycles round trip. The sub-bank stays busy for the read, the operation and the write.
l3:l3.atomic.source: docs/findings/05-claims.md:222, 224 (docs/reports/data/2026-09-22-hotline-aifoundry2/hotline.json); external/core-et/docs/CORE-ET-Shire-Cache-Specification.pdf pdf p.36 (busy rule 3), pdf p.40 §2.9, pdf p.72 §3.7.2
l3:l3.atomic.page: One hot line stops a shire

l3:l3.atomic-rails.statement: Atomics on home-L3 lines draw 3.99 W over idle on aifoundry2: 26% minion rail, 24% SRAM, 33% mesh, 17% unmetered.

l3:l3.flag.statement: A flag handed through global atomics costs 610-1,150 ns round trip (median 873) whatever the two shires' distance: it depends on which shire's L3 slice holds the flag's line.
l3:l3.flag.source: docs/reports/2026-09-18-et-soc1-on-chip-communication.html §'Latency grows with distance, except through memory'

l3:l3.leakage.statement: The SRAM rail at idle is 1.70 W at 67 C and 2.73 W at 82 C on aifoundry2 (slope 0.066 W/C on aifoundry3); at 80 C its 2.51 W is 19.6 mW per MB of the 128 MB of L2, L3 and scratchpad, an upper bound on the arrays' leakage since cache logic shares the rail. The L3's 32 MB are then at most about 0.63 W.
l3:l3.leakage.source: docs/energy-manual/04a-fine-grain.md:106-111 and its table (67 °C 1.698 W, 82 °C 2.726 W); docs/findings/05-claims.md:473
l3:l3.leakage.note: The 0.63 W for the L3 is a quarter of the rail, computed here.

l3:l3.observe.statement: No counter a user-mode kernel can read reports L3 hits or misses; the shire cache has per-bank performance monitors (events chosen by ESR) that need firmware or a new syscall, and an index CacheOp can read one quadword of any tag, state or data RAM with its ECC bits from M-mode.
l3:l3.observe.source: external/core-et/docs/CORE-ET-Shire-Cache-Specification.pdf pdf p.52 §2.15, pdf p.88-94 §3.14, pdf p.104 §4.9; workloads/memprobe/report_template.html:1063; docs/reports/sources/limits-of-observability.data.json ladder rows 'Chosen counter events', 'Raw SRAM row + ECC bits'

l3:l3.power-goal.statement: The spec's power line reads 'Power: TBD. Goal is 100 MW for the entire Shire Cache running benchmark' (presumably mW, per shire).

l3:l3.process.statement: TSMC 7 nm, 570 mm2, over 24 billion transistors (Esperanto's Hot Chips 33 slides and IEEE Micro 2022 paper).

l3:g.6t-cell.statement: GENERIC. A 6T SRAM cell stores a bit on two cross-coupled inverters (two PMOS pull-ups, two NMOS pull-downs) and connects to a bitline pair through two NMOS access transistors whose gates are the row's wordline.
l3:g.6t-cell.source: textbook (e.g. Rabaey, Digital Integrated Circuits, ch. 12)
l3:g.6t-cell.note: The ET-SoC-1 sources name the data array 'SRAM' but not its bitcell: u.bitcell.

l3:g.read.statement: GENERIC. A read: precharge/equalise PMOS hold both bitlines at the supply and switch off; the row decoder's NAND/NOR gates select one wordline driver, which raises that wordline across the row; in every cell of the row the access transistor on the side storing 0 pulls its bitline down through the pull-down NMOS, developing tens of mV; the column mux passes one pair per output bit to a latch-type sense amplifier, which fires on its enable and resolves to full rail into the output latch.
l3:g.read.note: Every column of the selected row discharges one bitline whatever the data, so the array's read energy is roughly data-independent; data-dependent energy comes from the output datapath, ECC and wires.

l3:g.write.statement: GENERIC. A write: write drivers pull one bitline of each selected pair to ground, the wordline rises, and the access transistor overpowers the cell's PMOS pull-up so the cell flips. Write assist (for example a negative bitline or a lowered cell supply) and a longer write pulse make the flip reliable at low voltage.
l3:g.write.note: The ET macros expose WA and WPULSE trims (l3.trim-table); which technique WA drives is not stated.

l3:g.assist.statement: GENERIC. Read assist usually lowers the wordline voltage so a read cannot flip a weak cell; read-margin settings delay the sense-amplifier enable so more bitline swing develops, slower but safer at low voltage.
l3:g.assist.note: The ET macros expose RA and RM (l3.trim-table); their exact circuit effect is vendor-specific.

l3:g.tag-compare.statement: GENERIC. Tag compare: per way, 23 XNOR gates (one per tag bit) feed an AND tree (or a precharged match line pulled down by any mismatch); the four hit signals select the way and encode it.

l3:g.ecc.statement: GENERIC. SECDED (72,64) Hamming code: 8 check bits per 64 data bits computed by XOR trees on write; on read a syndrome from the same XOR trees points at a single flipped bit, which an XOR corrects, and flags a double error.
l3:g.ecc.note: That the shire cache uses 8 ECC bits per 64-bit doubleword is et-spec (l3.geometry).

l3:g.icg.statement: GENERIC. An integrated clock gate is a latch (transparent while the clock is low) holding the enable, ANDed with the clock: when the enable is low the macro's clock does not toggle, so its clock tree and flops draw no switching power.

l3:g.crossing.statement: GENERIC. A voltage and clock crossing: a level shifter (cross-coupled PMOS over an NMOS differential input pair) lifts or drops the signal swing, and a 2-flip-flop synchroniser (as the spec's VCFIFO uses) samples it in the receiving clock, costing 2-3 receiving-clock cycles.
l3:g.crossing.source: textbook; the 2 stages are et-spec (external/core-et/docs/CORE-ET-Shire-Cache-Specification.pdf pdf p.11)

l3:g.router.statement: GENERIC. A mesh router stage: input virtual-channel buffers (flip-flop or register-file arrays), route computation, virtual-channel and switch allocators (arbiters), a crossbar of multiplexers, and output drivers onto the link; each link is a bundle of wires broken by repeaters (inverter pairs) every few hundred microns.
l3:g.router.source: textbook (Dally and Towles, Principles and Practices of Interconnection Networks)
l3:g.router.note: ET routers have 8 ports and 4 VC slots each, 9 main layers per stop (chip fact L105; SYNTHESIS.md:67-68).

l3:g.wire-energy.statement: GENERIC. A wire's switching energy is about C x V^2 per 0-to-1 transition (C about 0.2 pF/mm), so random data (a transition on about half the bits) costs several times zeros; repeaters add to it.

l3:g.leakage.statement: GENERIC. Every SRAM cell leaks all the time: sub-threshold current flows through its off transistors (one pull-up or pull-down per inverter and the access transistors), rising roughly exponentially with temperature.
l3:g.leakage.note: Matches the measured SRAM rail at idle (l3.leakage).

l3:g.no-refresh.statement: GENERIC. A 6T SRAM cell holds its bit as long as it is powered and needs no refresh; a 1T1C DRAM or eDRAM cell stores charge on a capacitor that leaks and must be refreshed every few tens of microseconds to milliseconds.
l3:g.no-refresh.note: Relevant to u.bitcell: the shire-cache spec describes no refresh (l3.no-refresh).

l3:u.bitcell.statement: UNKNOWN. What bitcell the shire-cache macros use (6T high-density? 8T? another cell?), and what the lab lead meant by 'not using SRAM'. The spec, the datasheet and the translation guide all call these arrays SRAM; the minion's L1 data array is a separate custom 1R1W macro (dcache_128x32_1r1w_lram) whose cell is not stated either.
l3:u.bitcell.source: external/core-et/docs/CORE-ET-Shire-Cache-Specification.pdf pdf p.48, p.51; external/et-man/ET Preliminary Datasheet Rev 1.0.pdf pdf p.4; external/core-et-main/AGENTS.md:609; external/core-et/rtl/libs/macros/dcache_128x32_1r1w_lram.v:5-12 (behavioural stand-in); external/core-et/rtl/shire/minion/dcache/dcache_data_ram_wrap.v
l3:u.bitcell.note: The lab lead's remark is not recorded in the repo; the owner relayed it.

l3:u.macro-geometry.statement: UNKNOWN. The physical organisation of mbd (4096 x 144), mbt (1024 x 116) and mbs (1024 x 40): rows, columns, column mux, internal banks, sense-amplifier type. Common compiler naming would read 'm4b4' as a 4:1 column mux and 4 banks, i.e. 256 wordlines x 576 bitline pairs per bank in mbd; nothing in the drop confirms it.

l3:u.live-settings.statement: UNKNOWN. The live values on these cards of esr_sc_ram_delay (default 2), esr_sc_zero_state_enable (default 1) and the RAM trims shire_cache_ram_cfg1/2 (emulator reset = RM0 row) at the 705 mV SRAM rail.

l3:u.rail-of-logic.statement: UNKNOWN. Whether the shire cache's logic (pipeline, crossbars, request queues, the high side of the VCFIFOs) is on the metered SRAM rail with the macros, or on another rail.
l3:u.rail-of-logic.source: external/core-et/docs/CORE-ET Minion Shire Description.pdf pdf p.10, p.18 (refers to the Power Spec)

l3:u.latency-split.statement: UNKNOWN. Where the 110-cycle L3 constant goes stage by stage, in particular the 61 ns that do not scale with the core clock (VCFIFO synchronisers, NoC bridges, mesh-stop entry and exit at 0 hops) and why the spec's 34 + 30 shire clocks exceed the measured 72 clock-scaled cycles.

l3:u.zero-share.statement: UNKNOWN. How much of the L3's zeros-vs-random saving (SRAM rail 2.9 vs 7.5 pJ/B) is the zero-state skip of the data macros and how much is data-dependent switching in the datapath, ECC and crossings.

l3:u.noc-hop.statement: UNKNOWN. The router pipeline per hop (4 NoC cycles each way is derived), which of the 9 main-NoC layers carries L3 requests and replies, and the flit width. The dimension order, asked here until 29 September, is measured (l3.route).

l3:u.slice-floorplan.statement: UNKNOWN. Where the four banks (and so the L3 slice's quarters) sit in the 3.7 mm shire tile relative to the mesh stop and the four L3-slave ports.
l3:u.slice-floorplan.source: external/core-et/docs/CORE-ET Minion Shire Description.pdf pdf p.5 Figure 1 (logical only)

l3:g.panel-read-count.statement: GENERIC, if each panel is an ordinary compiled SRAM macro: a line read raises one wordline in each of the 4 panels and fires 576 sense amplifiers (144 per panel); how many bitline pairs swing depends on the column mux, which the macro datasheets would settle.
l3:g.panel-read-count.source: textbook (GENERIC); widths from l2.seq.load-hit.09; the column mux is l2.macro.name-decode (unknown)

scp:scp.what.statement: The scratchpad is part of each shire's 4 MB shire cache configured as software-managed memory: no tags, never a miss, globally addressable by any agent; a request to another shire's slice leaves over the mesh and is served by that shire's L3-slave port.
scp:scp.what.source: external/core-et/docs/CORE-ET-Shire-Cache-Specification.pdf p.6 §1 (Overview), p.9-10 §1.1; external/et-man/ET Programmer's Reference Manual.pdf p.486 §15.3

scp:scp.size.statement: In mode M0, the reset mode and the one these cards run, each shire's scratchpad is 2.5 MB (640 of the 1,024 sets of every sub-bank), 80 MB over the 32 compute shires; the driver reports 81,920 KB on every card.
scp:scp.size.source: external/core-et/docs/CORE-ET-Shire-Cache-Specification.pdf p.21-22 Tables 6-7 ('The chip will come out of reset in mode M0'); external/et-platform/et-common-libs/include/system/layout.h:73 (0x280000); docs/reports/data/2026-09-22-cards/driver_config.json scp_kb

scp:scp.m0-rows.statement: M0 per sub-bank: scratchpad sets 0x000-0x27F (640), L2 sets 0x280-0x2FF (128), L3 sets 0x300-0x3FF (256). Scratchpad, L2 and L3 are row ranges of the same data panels, not separate memories: the scratchpad is the lowest 2,560 of each panel's 4,096 rows (set x 4 ways).
scp:scp.m0-rows.source: external/core-et/docs/CORE-ET-Shire-Cache-Specification.pdf p.22 Table 7 (Mode 0 base/end); external/core-et-main/hw/ip/shirecache/rtl/shirecache_pipe_sub_bank.sv:1613 (data RAM address = {set, way})
scp:scp.m0-rows.note: Row count derived: 640 sets x 4 ways. The base can be moved to skip faulty rows (external/core-et/docs/CORE-ET-Shire-Cache-Specification.pdf p.21), so 'rows 0-2559' assumes the M0 base 0x0.

scp:scp.addr.statement: Scratchpad address fields as a minion issues them (the PRM's format 0): [39:31] = 9'h1 (scratchpad region), [30] = 0 (the format bit), [29:23] the shire ID, 0x7F meaning the requester's own shire; then [22:12] set (bit 22 = 0 for a 4 MB build), [11:10] way, [9:8] sub-bank, [7:6] bank, [5:0] byte.
scp:scp.addr.source: external/et-man/ET Programmer's Reference Manual.pdf pdf p.486 §15.3 ('Format 0: Bit [30] set to 0 ... Shire ID is placed in bits [29:23]'; 'Shire ID[6:0] bits set to 7'b1111111 targets the local Shire'); external/core-et/docs/CORE-ET-Shire-Cache-Specification.pdf p.24 §1.4.1.3 (set, way, sub-bank, bank); external/core-et-main/hw/ip/shirecache/rtl/shirecache_pkg.sv:118, 146-149, 907
scp:scp.addr.note: The Shire Cache Specification v1.1 (p.24) gives the shire field as [30:23], all ones meaning local; the PRM says agents other than minions use that hardware format, with bit 30 a copy of bit 29.

scp:scp.addr-row.statement: So one 64 B scratchpad line lives at bank PA[7:6], sub-bank PA[9:8], panel row PA[21:10] of that sub-bank's four panels, 16 B per panel (quadword PA[5:4]). Consecutive lines rotate over the 4 banks and then the 4 sub-banks, so one 1 KB TensorLoad (16 consecutive lines) touches each of the shire cache's 16 sub-banks exactly once: 64 panel accesses.
scp:scp.addr-row.note: From the Ainekko re-implementation of the shire cache (core-et-main), which STATUS.md reports co-simulated against the original shire_cache RTL; that original is not in this checkout, and the open core-et drop is the Erbium branch. Treat as the design's behaviour, not a silicon measurement.

scp:scp.format1.statement: Format 1 (address bit 30 = 1, minions only) puts the shire ID in bits [29:28] and [10:6], so consecutive 64 B lines land in different shires' scratchpads.

scp:scp.banks.statement: Four banks per shire, each a quarter of the scratchpad, L2 and L3; each bank takes at most one request and returns at most one 512-bit line per cycle; each bank has four sub-banks.
scp:scp.banks.source: external/core-et/docs/CORE-ET-Shire-Cache-Specification.pdf p.6 §1, p.9 ('POR for the first SoC is 4M/Shire, 4 banks/Shire, 4 sub-banks/bank'), p.30 §2.1

scp:scp.always-hit.statement: A scratchpad read is 'always a hit': the pipeline does not read the tag or tag-state RAMs for it (both reads are squashed), takes the way from PA[11:10], and writes no LRU or state afterwards; the tag and tag-state panels stay idle on a scratchpad access.
scp:scp.always-hit.note: From the Ainekko re-implementation of the shire cache (core-et-main), which STATUS.md reports co-simulated against the original shire_cache RTL; that original is not in this checkout, and the open core-et drop is the Erbium branch. Treat as the design's behaviour, not a silicon measurement.

scp:scp.no-victims.statement: Scratchpad operations have no misses, no victims and no fills from below; Lock, Unlock, Flush and Evict to a local scratchpad address are not supported.
scp:scp.no-victims.source: external/core-et/docs/CORE-ET-Shire-Cache-Specification.pdf p.87 §3.13 ('For Scratchpad operations, there are no victims'), p.14-15 Table 2

scp:scp.xbar.statement: A full request crossbar joins the 4 neighbourhoods and the RBOX to the 4 banks and the UC block; an identical response crossbar returns lines; each bank has one catch FIFO per neighbourhood and a round-robin arbiter.

scp:scp.reqq.statement: Per bank: a 64-entry request queue (up to 21 entries reserved for L3-slave requests), a dataq entry per reqq entry, an 8-entry read buffer and a 32-entry coalescing buffer. Per sub-bank, L3-slave (remote) requests win the arbitration over neighbourhood requests.

scp:scp.pipe-stages.statement: A read passes ag (reqq allocate), ad, rqa (arbitration), tap, ta, ta0, ta1, te, tc (tag pipeline), dap, da, da0, da1 (data panel access, 2 cycles), de (ECC check and fix), dc (data complete, OR'ed across sub-banks, to the response mux). The pipeline is non-stalling; a sub-bank is busy for the panel access time, so it accepts a request every other cycle at the default timing.

scp:scp.ram-delay.statement: Tag, tag-state and data panel access time is 2, 3 or 4 shire-cache cycles, one control for all three (esr_sc_ram_delay); the design intends 2 and resets to 2 (reset value of sc_pipe_ctl 0x5C_FFFF_FFFF in the functional model decodes to ram_delay = 2, both read buffers and zero-state on).
scp:scp.ram-delay.note: What the cards actually run is not recorded anywhere we can read: see unknown scp.u-trim.

scp:scp.clock-gate.statement: The data panels' inputs are held still when not accessed, and the panel clock is gated on only around an access (for ram_delay cycles); a partial write enables only the quadword panels it writes.

scp:scp.rbuf.statement: Scratchpad reads install into the bank's 8-entry fully-associative read buffer (esr_sc_scp_rbuf_enable, on at reset), including reads that arrive from other shires; a repeat read of a clean line is served without touching the panels: 10 shire clocks against 21.

scp:scp.zero-state.statement: The shire cache's zero-state shortcut (no data-panel read or write when a line is all zeros, esr_sc_zero_state_enable) lives in the tag-state RAM, which scratchpad operations never read; so a scratchpad read of an all-zero line still reads the data panels, and a scratchpad write always writes them.
scp:scp.zero-state.note: From the Ainekko re-implementation of the shire cache (core-et-main), which STATUS.md reports co-simulated against the original shire_cache RTL; that original is not in this checkout, and the open core-et drop is the Erbium branch. Treat as the design's behaviour, not a silicon measurement. Consequence for the diagram: the measured zeros-vs-random difference of the own scratchpad cannot come from skipping the panels.

scp:scp.write-granule.statement: A scratchpad write counts as partial only below 16 B; 16 B and larger writes go straight to the panels with per-quadword enables, with no read-modify-write (L2 writes, by contrast, are partial unless a full line).
scp:scp.write-granule.note: From the Ainekko re-implementation of the shire cache (core-et-main), which STATUS.md reports co-simulated against the original shire_cache RTL; that original is not in this checkout, and the open core-et drop is the Erbium branch. Treat as the design's behaviour, not a silicon measurement.

scp:scp.idx-zero.statement: Each bank's index CacheOp state machine can walk a whole region, including 'SCP Zero' to clear the scratchpad, and gives debug read/write of any tag, state or data RAM word.

scp:scp.deep-sleep.statement: Tag-state, tag, data and dataq RAMs of a non-operational shire can be put in deep_sleep or shut_down by ESR (esr_sc_ram_deep_sleep / esr_sc_ram_shut_down, sc_pipe_ctl bits 41 and 40).

scp:scp.panel.statement: Data storage is built from 144-bit-wide 'SRAM memory panels' (128 data bits + 16 ECC bits), four per sub-bank, one per quadword of the 512-bit line. The data panel is named 'saduls0g4l1p4096x144m4b4w0c0p0d0s1rm0sdrw11', RAM type 1PUHD: 4,096 words x 144 bits.
scp:scp.panel.source: external/core-et/docs/CORE-ET-Shire-Cache-Specification.pdf p.48 §2.14.5 ('SRAM memory panels that are 144 bits wide'), p.51 (data_ram (mbd) = saduls0g4l1p4096x144m4b4w0c0p0d0s1rm0sdrw11 (1PUHD)); external/core-et/rtl/inc/shire_cache_defines.vh:362 (SC_MBD_DATA_SIZE = 576/4)
scp:scp.panel.note: The spec is version 1.1 and also covers later chips (sections marked Nemi, Gepardo); the macro table is not labelled per chip. Its 4096x144 matches the 4 MB ET-SoC-1 geometry.

scp:scp.panel-others.statement: Other shire-cache macros: tag RAM 'saduls0g4l1p1024x116m4b1...' (1PUHD, 4 ways x (23-bit tag + 6 ECC)), tag-state RAM 'saculs0g4l2p1024x40m4b1...' (2PUHDRF, two-ported by the spec), I-cache data 'saduls0g4l1p512x144m4b1...'. The scratchpad path uses only the data panels.
scp:scp.panel-others.source: external/core-et/docs/CORE-ET-Shire-Cache-Specification.pdf p.47 §2.14.2-2.14.3, p.51 Tables 13-14, p.45 ('the state RAM is two-ported')

scp:scp.panel-count.statement: Per shire 64 data panels (4 banks x 4 sub-banks x 4), each 589,824 bits; 37.7 Mbit per shire including ECC (32 Mbit data + 4 Mbit ECC); 2,048 data panels over the 32 compute shires.
scp:scp.panel-count.note: If each bit is a 6-transistor cell (GENERIC assumption, see scp.u-cell) that is 3.54 M transistors per panel array and about 226 M per shire, cells only.

scp:scp.line-read-panels.statement: A full 64 B scratchpad read raises one row in each of the four quadword panels of one sub-bank and senses 576 bits (512 data + 64 ECC); the other 15 sub-banks, and the tag and tag-state panels, stay idle.
scp:scp.line-read-panels.note: From the Ainekko re-implementation of the shire cache (core-et-main), which STATUS.md reports co-simulated against the original shire_cache RTL; that original is not in this checkout, and the open core-et drop is the Erbium branch. Treat as the design's behaviour, not a silicon measurement.

scp:scp.vendor.statement: The panels are third-party IP; their memory test is a shared-bus BIST 'such as the Synopsys SMS (STAR Memory System)' with logical RAMs mbs (tag state), mbt (tag), mbd (data), mbq (dataq), mbi (I-cache). The RTL build files call them 'physical SRAM macros' and note 'Synopsis memories not available' for synthesis.
scp:scp.vendor.note: No source names the memory compiler or the bitcell outright; the 'sa..ls0g4' prefix is a compiler naming convention we cannot decode from these sources (scp.u-macro).

scp:scp.prm-sram-family.statement: The PRM calls the same macro families SRAMs: the Maxion shire has configuration registers 'sacrls_config', 'sadcls_config', 'saduls_config', 'sadrls_config' - 'Configuration bits for SADULS SRAM's. Bits 17:0 control read and write margins, bias control, etc.'
scp:scp.prm-sram-family.source: external/et-man/ET Programmer's Reference Manual.pdf p.346 Table 15-5 (R_MX_SRAM_RM)

scp:scp.trim-knobs.statement: Each logical RAM group has trim bits set by ESR shire_cache_ram_cfg1-4 (cfg2 = data panels): RM[3:0] read margin, RME, RA[1:0] read assist, WA[2:0] write assist, WPULSE[2:0] write pulse, BC[2:0] (bias control), TEST1, TEST_RNM. 'The RAM macros have trim bits to allow them to operate at various voltage levels... The ESR settings default to RM0 mode to allow nominal 650mV operation.'

scp:scp.trim-reset.statement: Data-panel trim at reset: WA = 7, RA = 1, RM = 0, RME = 0 (ESR value 0x3A0 in the functional model), i.e. the RM0 'nominal 650 mV' row of Table 14.

scp:scp.fw-no-trim.statement: Nothing in the open firmware writes the RAM-trim ESRs or esr_sc_ram_delay: in et-platform they appear only in the register headers and the functional model's reset values. Unless closed boot code changes them, the panels run at reset trim and 2-cycle timing.
scp:scp.fw-no-trim.source: grep of external/et-platform/ for ram_cfg / RAM_CFG / SC_PIPE_CTL / ram_delay: hits only in sw-sysemu/esrs_et.cpp, sw-sysemu/esrs.h, etsoc-hal/include/hwinc/etsoc_shire_cache_esr.h, et-common-libs/include/etsoc/isa/esr_defines.h
scp:scp.fw-no-trim.note: An absence in the open tree, not a reading from a card; see scp.u-trim.

scp:scp.ecc.statement: SECDED on everything: 8 ECC bits per 64-bit data word (576 bits stored per 512-bit line), checked and corrected in stage de; ECC scrubbing is a reserved bit on this chip ('Future chips will implement this feature').

scp:scp.rail.statement: The shire-cache arrays sit on their own SRAM rail: set point 705 mV, 701-707 mV on die, against 518-520 mV for the minions and 484-485 mV for the mesh (aifoundry2 telemetry).

scp:scp.rail-margin.statement: The 705 mV rail is 120 mV above the data panels' RM0 Vmin (585 mV) and 55 mV above RM0's 650 mV nominal.

scp:scp.regulator.statement: The SRAM rail ('SRAM, aka: SCW voltage regulator') is a Linear Technologies LTM4680 PMBus module rated 60 A; the PMIC meters it with the minion and NoC rails.
scp:scp.regulator.source: external/et-man/ET-PCIe-Dev-Card-V3.pdf p.5-6 (Key Voltage Regulators); docs/findings/05-claims.md:337; docs/findings/01-resources.md:202-211 (R13)

scp:scp.hv-region.statement: The Shire Channel (shire cache, UC block, I-cache data memory) runs at high voltage: the I-cache data memory sits there 'because it has to be operated at high voltage'. Each neighbourhood is split into a low-voltage region (minions, neighbourhood clock) and a high-voltage interface region on the shire clock, joined by a semi-synchronous interface; level shifters and voltage-crossing FIFOs separate the domains.
scp:scp.hv-region.source: external/core-et/docs/CORE-ET Minion Shire Description.pdf p.4, p.10 §3.1, p.18 §5; external/core-et/docs/CORE-ET-Neigborhood-MAS.pdf p.6 §2; external/core-et/rtl/libs/mems_and_fifos/vclevel_shft_l2h.v, vcfifo_wr_hiv_gcd.v
scp:scp.hv-region.note: Which regulator feeds the 'high voltage' region is not stated; the 705 mV SRAM rail is the only candidate among the metered ones (scp.u-rail).

scp:scp.clocks.statement: Shire logic runs on shire_clock from the shire's own PLL, the neighbourhoods on a DLL copy shifted 180 degrees; the mesh on clk__noc from PLL2 (design 500 MHz). Telemetry on these cards reports minion 600 MHz and NoC 400 MHz; it does not report the shire-cache clock.
scp:scp.clocks.source: external/core-et/docs/CORE-ET Minion Shire Description.pdf p.12 Table 2; horace-telemetry.jsonl mhz.minion, mhz.noc

scp:scp.clock-ratio.statement: The read buffer saves 11 cycles in both units: the spec's 10 vs 21 shire clocks, and the measured 36 vs 47 minion cycles. That fits a shire-cache clock equal to the 600 MHz minion clock, which would make a 2-cycle panel access 3.3 ns.
scp:scp.clock-ratio.note: An inference from a difference; see scp.u-clock.

scp:scp.lat-own.statement: A load that misses the L1 and hits the shire's own scratchpad: 47.00 cycles load-to-use (78 ns at 600 MHz), the same as an L2 hit; a read-buffer hit 36.00; hart 1 pays 3 more (50 and 39). Identical on three cards.

scp:scp.lat-split.statement: Of the 47 cycles, the spec accounts for 21 shire clocks inside the shire cache including both crossbars; the other ~26 are the minion pipeline, the L1 miss and the neighbourhood's request (at least 6 clocks for a minion) and response (at least 6 clocks to a minion) paths.

scp:scp.same-as-l2.statement: The scratchpad is the L2 without the tags: same 47-cycle latency, same read buffer, same 4.0 B per minion-cycle; pass by pass the L2-minus-scratchpad energy difference included zero on each of three cards. Skipping the tag panels saves no time because the pipeline stages are fixed.
scp:scp.same-as-l2.note: The latency and bandwidth parts are measured; 'saves no time because the stages are fixed' is derived from the spec's non-stalling pipeline.

scp:scp.lat-remote.statement: Another shire's scratchpad: 99.84 + 12.00 cycles per mesh hop at 600 MHz (112-220 cycles, 186-366 ns over 1-10 hops); all 124 points within one cycle; a to b equals b to a within 0.032 cycles, on three cards.

scp:scp.lat-remote-split.statement: Fitted over 600, 700 and 800 MHz, a remote scratchpad load is 65.95 minion cycles + 56.48 ns + 20.00 ns per hop: the part that scales with the core clock (both shires' pipelines) and a fixed part in other clock domains (mesh, clock crossings).

scp:scp.lat-leave.statement: Leaving the shire costs about 53 cycles before the first hop (99.84 at zero hops against 47 locally); each hop then adds 12 minion cycles round trip = 20 ns = 8 cycles of the 400 MHz mesh clock, 4 each way.

scp:scp.tl-one.statement: One minion's TensorLoad from its own scratchpad into its L1 scratchpad: 4 lines 43.0 cycles, 8 lines 80.1, 16 lines 160.1 (the L2: 41.9 and 160.4 for 4 and 16), on each of three cards.

scp:scp.tl-pipelining.statement: Each extra line costs 10.0 cycles ((160.1 - 80.1) / 8), which is 4 transfers in flight over a ~40-cycle round trip: the tensor-load unit keeps up to 4 L2 transfers outstanding.

scp:scp.bw-own.statement: All 1,024 minions tensor-loading their own shire's scratchpad: 2.46 TB/s, 4.0 B per minion-cycle = 128 B per shire-cycle = 2 lines per shire-cycle, half the four banks' 256 B per cycle.

scp:scp.bw-one-neigh.statement: With only one neighbourhood per shire reading, the chip still moves 966-967 GB/s: about 50 B per shire-cycle for 8 minions, where four neighbourhoods together get 128.

scp:scp.bw-bank-stride.statement: 64 B tensor loads striding 64 or 128 B stream at 923 GB/s; striding 256 B, which returns to the same bank every time, 614 GB/s (-33%) on every card; energy per byte indistinguishable.

scp:scp.bw-store.statement: Tensor stores into the own scratchpad: 1.23 TB/s, half the read rate.

scp:scp.bw-remote.statement: Every shire reading the scratchpad 16 shire IDs away (2.1 mesh hops on average): 0.96 TB/s, 1.56 B per minion-cycle.

scp:scp.bw-spec-port.statement: Upstream of the bank, a neighbourhood's 8 minions share one 512-bit ET-Link; its Fill FIFO delivers at most one response per cycle and, to one agent, one every other cycle; each minion's response port is 256 bits, so a 64 B line takes it two cycles.

scp:scp.e-own.statement: Reading the own scratchpad by 1 KB tensor loads at 600 MHz, above idle: 2.25 pJ/B [2.06-2.61] when it holds zeros, 4.40 [3.94-5.08] when it holds random data (three passes on each of three cards).

scp:scp.e-catalogue.statement: Catalogue: tensor load from the own scratchpad 2.12 / 4.43 pJ/B (zeros / random), tensor store into it 4.65 / 8.58: a scratchpad write costs about twice a read.

scp:scp.e-rails-load.statement: Where the power of an own-scratchpad tensor-load stream goes (aifoundry2, random, 10.19 W over idle): 69% SRAM rail, 24% minion rail, 1% mesh, 7% on no meter. Tensor store (9.83 W): 76% SRAM, 20% minions, 1% mesh, 3% unmetered.

scp:scp.e-sram-line.statement: On the SRAM rail alone, reading the own scratchpad costs 2.84 pJ/B on random data and 1.44 on zeros (aifoundry2; aifoundry3 2.82 / 1.43; aifoundry1-c1 2.41 / 1.23): 182 and 92 pJ per 64 B line, about 46 and 23 pJ per panel access, 0.32 pJ per stored bit read on random data.
scp:scp.e-sram-line.unit: pJ per 64 B line on the SRAM rail (random, aifoundry2)
scp:scp.e-sram-line.note: Rail watts over idle divided by bytes per second at 2,458 GB/s. Includes everything on that rail, which may be more than the arrays (scp.u-rail). The PMIC's running average reaches 0.94 of a step by the read window, so rail values may be up to 6% low (docs/energy-manual/04a-fine-grain.md:158). aifoundry1-c1 reads lower on this rail and higher on the minion rail.

scp:scp.e-sram-write.statement: On the SRAM rail, writing the own scratchpad by tensor store costs 6.08 pJ/B random and 3.27 zeros (aifoundry2): 389 and 209 pJ per 64 B line, 2.1x and 2.3x a read of the same data.
scp:scp.e-sram-write.unit: pJ per 64 B line on the SRAM rail (write, random, aifoundry2)
scp:scp.e-sram-write.note: No read-modify-write is involved for writes of 16 B or more (scp.write-granule), so the factor is the write itself plus its request path.

scp:scp.e-data.statement: Random data costs 2.0x zeros on the SRAM rail for a scratchpad read (2.84 vs 1.44 pJ/B, aifoundry2): 90 pJ more per line. Since the zero-state shortcut does not apply to the scratchpad (scp.zero-state), the panels are read either way; the difference is what toggles with the data.
scp:scp.e-data.unit: pJ per line, random minus zeros (SRAM rail)
scp:scp.e-data.note: Where it toggles (bitcell array, macro read path, ECC, pipeline, crossbar) cannot be told from rail power: scp.u-rail and scp.u-macro.

scp:scp.e-l1fill.statement: Filling one 64 B line from the scratchpad into the L1 costs 101 pJ on zeros and 238 pJ on random data (1.6 and 3.7 pJ per byte of line); what random data adds, about 138 pJ per line, is 269 fJ per bit on the path from the shire cache into the L1.

scp:scp.e-neigh.statement: Which neighbourhood reads makes little difference: 4.14, 3.93, 4.25, 4.25 pJ/B for neighbourhoods 0-3 (random).

scp:scp.e-remote.statement: Another shire's scratchpad (16 IDs away, 2.1 hops on average): 5.10 pJ/B [4.40-6.45] on zeros, 11.8 [9.5-14.4] on random data.

scp:scp.e-hop.statement: Each mesh hop adds 0.67 pJ/B on zeros and 1.80 on random data (1-8 hop fit; 2.2-2.4 on random over 1-6 hops): 142 fJ per random bit per hop. Leaving the shire costs about one more hop.

scp:scp.e-rails-remote.statement: Rail split of a remote scratchpad read (aifoundry2, random): 1 hop 14% minions / 50% SRAM / 27% mesh / 10% unmetered; 3 hops 11/36/40/14; 6 hops 8/26/50/17. The mesh rail alone: 1.27 pJ/B per hop.
scp:scp.e-rails-remote.unit: % on the mesh rail at 6 hops

scp:scp.gather.statement: Random 4 B gathers (fgw.ps) from the own scratchpad: 27.4 G elements/s at 367.8 pJ each, the same rate as the L2 because each element fetches its own line and a minion has two miss handlers; from a scratchpad 2 hops away 10.2 G/s at 903 pJ.

scp:scp.leak.statement: The SRAM rail at idle (all 128 MB of L2, L3 and scratchpad plus whatever else is on it): 2.51 W at 80 C on aifoundry2, 19.6 mW per MB, an upper bound on the arrays' leakage; a byte held for one second leaks at most ~19 nJ, as much as reading it 4,200 times. aifoundry3 and aifoundry1-c1 sit about 1 W higher.

scp:scp.power-goal.statement: The spec's power goal is '100 MW [sic] for the entire Shire Cache running benchmark'; streaming random data from the own scratchpad raises the SRAM rail 6.99 W over idle on aifoundry2, 218 mW per shire.
scp:scp.power-goal.source: external/core-et/docs/CORE-ET-Shire-Cache-Specification.pdf p.11 ('Power: TBD. Goal is 100 MW'); docs/reports/data/2026-09-23-energy-manual/catalogue.json aifoundry2 tload/scp/random
scp:scp.power-goal.note: The goal presumably means mW; its benchmark and clock are not stated.

scp:scp.vendor-virus.statement: Esperanto's own worst case for the SRAM ('SCW') regulator is a scratchpad kernel: scw_power_virus streams random data between the L1 scratchpad and the local L2 scratchpad (0xBF800000, the 'self' shire) with TensorLoad and TensorStore on shires 0-31.

scp:scp.tensorload.statement: TensorLoad (CSR 0x83F, hart 0 only) reads up to 16 rows of 64 B (row stride in x31) and writes them into consecutive L1-scratchpad lines, bypassing the L1 data cache; TensorLoad Setup B streams lines into a 4-entry VPU buffer instead (TenB).
scp:scp.tensorload.source: external/et-man/ET Programmer's Reference Manual.pdf p.264, p.275; external/core-et/docs/Minion DCache Description.pdf p.40-43 §3.9

scp:scp.tl-dest.statement: The destination of a TensorLoad is latch RAM, not SRAM: the minion's L1 data cache (and the L1 scratchpad carved from it) is 4 LRAM (latch-RAM) blocks of 128 rows x 64 bits.
scp:scp.tl-dest.source: external/core-et/docs/Minion DCache Description.pdf p.29-30 ('The physical memory of the DCache is made of 4 LRAM (Latch-RAM) blocks'); external/core-et/rtl/libs/macros/dcache_128x32_1r1w_lram.v
scp:scp.tl-dest.note: Relevant to the lab lead's 'not SRAM': the L1 is documented as latches, the shire cache as SRAM panels (scp.u-cell).

scp:scp.coop.statement: Cooperative TensorLoad: identical requests from minions across a shire's neighbourhoods are synchronised and sent as one ReadCoop; the bank's response mux broadcasts the line to every cooperating neighbourhood.
scp:scp.coop.source: external/core-et/docs/CORE-ET-Neigborhood-MAS.pdf p.23-24 §4.5; external/core-et/docs/CORE-ET-Shire-Cache-Specification.pdf p.58 §3.3; external/et-man/ET Programmer's Reference Manual.pdf p.273 §9.3.1.1

scp:scp.tl-l2scp.statement: TensorLoadL2Scp (CSR 0x85F; hart 1 may issue it) copies up to 16 lines from memory into this shire's L2 scratchpad, bypassing the L1 and L2; in the bank it is REQ_ScpFill: a mesh read of the source (L3, DRAM or a remote scratchpad), then an SCP_Fill write. The source address must use the real shire ID, not the self ID (erratum RTLMIN-6579).
scp:scp.tl-l2scp.source: external/et-man/ET Programmer's Reference Manual.pdf p.264, p.289-290; external/core-et/docs/CORE-ET-Shire-Cache-Specification.pdf p.15, p.87 §3.13; external/et-man/ET-SoC Errata.pdf p.83 §4.4

scp:scp.remote-write.statement: Writes to another shire's scratchpad: a plain write goes from the dataq to the mesh without using the local pipeline; a TensorStore write-around is coalesced in the local L2 and sent when the line is full (a full-line write-around that misses bypasses the local data panels); the target shire's L3 slave writes its scratchpad through its pipeline. Such write-arounds are not ordered against other remote scratchpad accesses (erratum RTLMIN-6617).
scp:scp.remote-write.source: external/core-et/docs/CORE-ET-Shire-Cache-Specification.pdf p.13 Table 2, p.40 §2.7, p.62 §3.4.5, §3.5; external/et-man/ET-SoC Errata.pdf p.84 §4.6; external/core-et-main/hw/ip/shirecache/rtl/shirecache_pipe_sub_bank.sv:640-642, 810

scp:scp.relay.statement: Handing each stage's output to the next shire's scratchpad instead of DRAM: 592.5 GB/s against 47.7 (12.4x), own scratchpad 1,487 GB/s (31x); energy per byte moved 116.2 / 8.92 / 4.34 pJ/B (DRAM / next shire / own), DRAM over next shire 12.9-13.1x on every card.
scp:scp.relay.page: Hand it to the next shire

scp:scp.relay-mech.statement: In the relay kernel, a 'next shire' stage reads the previous shire's scratchpad with 32 B vector loads through the L1 (remote scratchpad reads over the mesh) and writes its own scratchpad with TensorStores of 32 B rows.

scp:scp.atomic.statement: A global atomic on a scratchpad word is performed by the home bank's atomic block (read, ALU, write; the sub-bank is held busy throughout) after arriving on the L3-slave port; the bank retires one every 10.00 cycles; an uncontended remote atomic takes 216 cycles round trip; an atomic through the self ID 0x7F is a bus error.
scp:scp.atomic.unit: cycles per atomic at the bank
scp:scp.atomic.source: external/core-et/docs/CORE-ET-Shire-Cache-Specification.pdf p.17 (L3 slave REQ_Atomic, local SCP), p.36, p.40 §2.9; docs/findings/05-claims.md:232; docs/findings/17-hot-line.md:35-38; lat.json [item=LAT-H]
scp:scp.atomic.page: One hot line stops a shire

scp:scp.starve.statement: Because remote (L3-slave) requests win each sub-bank's arbitration, 22 or more minions of one other shire hammering one scratchpad word stop the host shire's own scratchpad reads (0.02% of their rate); 21 leave it at 95.6%. Errata RTLMIN-6207 and -6214 describe it.
scp:scp.starve.source: docs/findings/05-claims.md:427; docs/findings/17-hot-line.md:44-95; external/core-et/docs/CORE-ET-Shire-Cache-Specification.pdf p.36; external/et-man/ET-SoC Errata.pdf p.80
scp:scp.starve.page: One hot line stops a shire

scp:scp.offset0.statement: Offset 0 of a shire's scratchpad faulted during development (card not recorded); the relay's buffers start at 256 KB.
scp:scp.offset0.page: Hand it to the next shire

scp:scp.g-cell.statement: GENERIC. A 6T SRAM cell stores a bit in two cross-coupled CMOS inverters (2 PMOS pull-ups, 2 NMOS pull-downs); two NMOS access (pass-gate) transistors, gated by the wordline, connect the two storage nodes to the bitline pair BL/BLB.
scp:scp.g-cell.source: GENERIC (textbook single-port 6T SRAM; not from an ET source)

scp:scp.g-read.statement: GENERIC. A read: precharge PMOS and an equaliser hold BL and BLB at VDD, then release; the row decoder's wordline driver raises one wordline; on the side storing 0, the access and pull-down NMOS discharge that bitline by some tens of millivolts to ~100 mV; the column mux passes the selected pairs to sense amplifiers; sense-enable fires a latch-type amplifier (cross-coupled pair with an NMOS tail) that resolves the small difference to full swing into an output latch; the wordline falls and the precharge restores the bitlines.
scp:scp.g-read.source: GENERIC (textbook single-port 6T SRAM; not from an ET source)

scp:scp.g-read-data.statement: GENERIC. In a differential read exactly one bitline of each pair discharges whether the cell holds 0 or 1, so the array's read energy is to first order independent of the data; data dependence comes from what follows the sense amplifiers (outputs that toggle, buses, ECC) unless the macro uses a precharged single-ended global read line.
scp:scp.g-read-data.source: GENERIC (textbook single-port 6T SRAM; not from an ET source)

scp:scp.g-half-select.statement: GENERIC. With column multiplexing, every cell on the raised wordline discharges its bitline, not only the columns being read: with a 4:1 mux, four bitline pairs swing for every bit delivered (the unread three are 'half-selected').
scp:scp.g-half-select.source: GENERIC (textbook single-port 6T SRAM; not from an ET source)
scp:scp.g-half-select.note: Whether the 'm4' in the ET macro name means a 4:1 column mux is unknown (scp.u-macro).

scp:scp.g-write.statement: GENERIC. A write: write drivers pull one bitline of each selected column fully to ground, the wordline rises, the access transistor overpowers the cell's pull-up and the cell flips; write assist (e.g. a negative bitline boost) and the wordline pulse width set the margin. Restoring a full-swing bitline costs more than a small-swing read.
scp:scp.g-write.source: GENERIC (textbook single-port 6T SRAM; not from an ET source)
scp:scp.g-write.note: The ET macros expose WA (write assist) and WPULSE knobs (scp.trim-knobs); what circuit each drives is not stated.

scp:scp.g-assist.statement: GENERIC. Read-margin trims adjust the self-timed sense-enable delay (often from a replica bitline); read assist lowers the wordline voltage to protect the cell from read upset. These are standard knobs of FinFET-era SRAM compilers.
scp:scp.g-assist.source: GENERIC (textbook single-port 6T SRAM; not from an ET source)

scp:scp.g-static.statement: GENERIC. SRAM is static: no refresh, the bit holds as long as the rail is up; its standing cost is leakage through the off transistors, which rises steeply with temperature; retention (deep-sleep) modes lower the array voltage.
scp:scp.g-static.source: GENERIC (textbook single-port 6T SRAM; not from an ET source)

scp:scp.g-ecc.statement: GENERIC. A SECDED code with 8 check bits per 64 data bits (e.g. Hsiao (72,64)) corrects one bit and detects two; for linear codes, all-zero data has all-zero check bits.
scp:scp.g-ecc.note: Which code the shire cache uses is not stated.

scp:scp.g-level-shifter.statement: GENERIC. A low-to-high level shifter (0.52 V minion domain to a higher domain) is typically a cross-coupled PMOS pair driven by NMOS input transistors.
scp:scp.g-level-shifter.note: The ET RTL models its level shifter as a buffer (external/core-et/rtl/libs/mems_and_fifos/vclevel_shft_l2h.v); the physical cell is not given.

scp:scp.u-cell.statement: What storage cell is in the shire-cache data panels on ET-SoC-1 silicon? The Shire Cache Specification calls them 'SRAM memory panels' (p.48) named saduls0g4l1p4096x144m4b4... type 1PUHD (p.51) and the PRM calls the SADULS family SRAMs (p.346), but the lab lead says the chip does not use SRAM. If not a 6T SRAM cell, what is it (8T or register-file cell, latch array, gain cell or eDRAM)? The L1 data cache is documented as latch RAM (DCache Description p.29) - is that what was meant?
scp:scp.u-cell.source: open question: not settled by any source in the repo, external/ or the published pages
scp:scp.u-cell.note: Settles: The transistor-level drawing of the scratchpad, L2 and L3 array: 6 transistors per bit with a differential bitline pair and a sense amplifier, or another cell; and whether reads are destructive or need refresh (which would add a refresh step to this level's sequence).

scp:scp.u-macro.statement: What is the data panel's physical organisation? Decode the macro name saduls0g4l1p4096x144m4b4w0c0p0d0s1rm0sdrw11 (compiler, 'm4' column mux?, 'b4' internal banks?), and give rows x columns per sub-array, bitline length, and whether the read path uses a precharged global read bus. The macro datasheet or .lib would settle it (see rung 19, a cell library).
scp:scp.u-macro.source: open question: not settled by any source in the repo, external/ or the published pages
scp:scp.u-macro.note: Settles: How many wordlines, bitline pairs and sense amplifiers switch per 144-bit panel access (e.g. 576 bitline pairs swing for 144 bits read if 4:1), and where the data-dependent part of the read energy sits (array or periphery).

scp:scp.u-rail.statement: Which circuits does the 705 mV SRAM ('SCW') regulator feed: only the memory macros, or the whole Shire Channel (the shire-cache pipeline, queues, crossbars, ECC, the UC block, the neighbourhoods' high-voltage interface region)? The Power Spec that the Shire Description cites (§5) would say (see ask-design-docs).
scp:scp.u-rail.source: open question: not settled by any source in the repo, external/ or the published pages
scp:scp.u-rail.note: Settles: How the measured 69% SRAM-rail share of a scratchpad read (182 pJ per line on random data) is split between the bitcell array and the logic around it: the colour of each block in the energy view, and whether the zeros-vs-random difference belongs to the array or to the datapath.

scp:scp.u-trim.statement: What panel timing and trim do the cards run? esr_sc_ram_delay (2, 3 or 4 cycles; resets to 2) and shire_cache_ram_cfg1-4 (reset for the data panels: RM 0, RME 0, WA 7, RA 1 = Table 14's RM0 '650 mV nominal' row). The open firmware never writes them; does boot ROM or BL1 change them for the 705 mV rail? A one-time M-mode read of ESR 0x55 on each card would also settle it.
scp:scp.u-trim.source: open question: not settled by any source in the repo, external/ or the published pages
scp:scp.u-trim.note: Settles: The panel access time drawn in the pipeline (2 cycles = 3.3 ns at 600 MHz) and which read-margin and write-assist mode the transistor animation shows.

scp:scp.clock.statement: The shire cache runs on shire_clock, the minion clock (the neighbourhood clock is shire_clock shifted 180 degrees), so at 600 MHz on these cards: one shire-cache cycle is one minion cycle. The read buffer's measured saving, 11 minion cycles (47 against 36), matches the spec's 21 against 10 shire clocks at 1:1.
scp:scp.clock.source: external/core-et/docs/CORE-ET Minion Shire Description.pdf pdf p.12 Table 2; external/et-man/ET-SoC Errata.pdf pdf p.42; external/core-et/docs/CORE-ET-Shire-Cache-Specification.pdf p.11 Table 1; scp.lat-own
scp:scp.clock.note: As l2.clock and l3.clock state; the telemetry reports only the minion and NoC clocks.

scp:scp.u-bw.statement: What limits the own-scratchpad stream to 128 B per shire-cycle (2.46 TB/s chip-wide), half of four banks x 64 B? The candidates are the sub-bank busy time, the response crossbar, the neighbourhood's Fill FIFO and 512-bit link, or the minions' 256-bit response ports; one neighbourhood alone reaches about 50 B per cycle.
scp:scp.u-bw.source: open question: not settled by any source in the repo, external/ or the published pages
scp:scp.u-bw.note: Settles: Which block the diagram highlights as the bottleneck when all 1,024 minions stream a TensorLoad.

scp:scp.u-remote-split.statement: Where do the ~53 extra cycles of a remote scratchpad read go (99.84 cycles at zero hops against 47 locally; 65.95 cycles + 56.48 ns): the to_l3 mesh master and its voltage-crossing FIFOs, the mesh stops, the target's L3-slave FIFO and reqq, the return path? The NoC reference manual (ask-noc-docs) and the shire cache's per-block latencies would split it.
scp:scp.u-remote-split.source: open question: not settled by any source in the repo, external/ or the published pages
scp:scp.u-remote-split.note: Settles: Per-block latency labels on the remote-read path, the one part of this level whose timing is drawn from a fit rather than from parts.

dram:dram.topo.memshires.statement: Eight memory shires, four on the west side (0-3) and four on the east side (4-7) of the die, each driving two 16-bit LPDDR4X channels: 16 channels in all.
dram:dram.topo.memshires.source: external/et-man/ET Programmer's Reference Manual.pdf pdf p.17 §1.5 (txt line 544-548); external/et-man/ET Preliminary Datasheet Rev 1.0.pdf pdf p.30 §7 and §7.1
dram:dram.topo.memshires.note: West 0-3 / east 4-7 is the PRM's and the firmware's naming; the latency fit's logical map draws them above and below the grid (chip-diagram fact fw.memshires).

dram:dram.topo.packages.statement: Four LPDDR4X packages on the card, each with four 16-bit channels (64 bits per package, 256 bits in all); two memory shires share each package.
dram:dram.topo.packages.source: external/et-man/ET Programmer's Reference Manual.pdf pdf p.17 §1.5; external/et-man/ET Preliminary Datasheet Rev 1.0.pdf pdf p.30 §7 ('Two Memshires communicate with each 64-bit LPDDR4X memory device'); external/et-man/ET-PCIe-Dev-Card-V3.pdf pdf p.3 ('4 x LPDDR4x DRAM devices for a combined 256-bit memory interface')
dram:dram.topo.packages.note: The datasheet's §2.2.2 (pdf p.16) calls each package a 'bank' ('four banks of LPDDR4X memory. Each bank is controlled by two Memory Shires'): not a DRAM bank. The diagram should say 'package'.

dram:dram.topo.pkg-pairing.statement: Which two memory shires share each LPDDR4X package is not documented; the chip diagram pairs neighbours (0-1, 2-3, 4-5, 6-7) on an assumption.
dram:dram.topo.pkg-pairing.source: external/et-man/ET Preliminary Datasheet Rev 1.0.pdf pdf p.30 §7; docs/reports/data/2026-09-27-chip-diagram/facts.json facts['dram.pkg-pairing']; hub ask 'ask-card-schematic' (docs/reports/sources/limits-of-observability.data.json improvements[24])

dram:dram.topo.controllers.statement: Each memory shire holds two Synopsys uMCTL2 DDR controller instances, one per 16-bit channel: the firmware programs controller blocks 0 and 1 of every memory shire, and the memory shire has separate mode-register read-back registers for 'memory controller 0' and 'memory controller 1'.
dram:dram.topo.controllers.source: external/et-man/ET Programmer's Reference Manual.pdf pdf p.17 §1.5 ('connected to two memory controllers that each have a 16-bit LPPDR4X channel'); external/et-man/ET Programmer's Reference Manual.pdf pdf p.515 Table 15-90 (ddrc_u0_mrr_data, ddrc_u1_mrr_data); external/et-platform/device-bootloaders/src/ServiceProcessorBL2/utils/mem_controller_utils.c:83-88 (get_ddrc_address: block 1 at +0x1000), :604-607 (ms_write_both_ddrc_reg); external/et-man/ET-SoC Errata.pdf pdf p.88 (errata 5.2 cites the uMCTL2 Databook v3.50a)
dram:dram.topo.controllers.note: The datasheet disagrees: 'two 16-bit LPDDR4X physical interfaces sharing a single 32-bit controller' (external/et-man/ET Preliminary Datasheet Rev 1.0.pdf pdf p.30 §7). Firmware and PRM agree on two controllers; see dram.topo.phy and the ask.

dram:dram.topo.phy.statement: One DDR PHY per memory shire serves both channels: the firmware writes one PHY training message block per memory shire, with the DRAM's MR14 (VREF-DQ) set for 'Channel A' and 'Channel B'; the open RTL gives the memory shire's DDR subsystem 4 data-byte lanes (DBYTEs, 2 per 16-bit channel), 6 address/command blocks (ANIBs) and a 16-bit DRAM data width.
dram:dram.topo.phy.source: external/et-platform/device-bootloaders/src/ServiceProcessorBL2/driver/mem_controller.c:190-192 (ms_patch_phy_ram_before_training); external/et-platform/device-bootloaders/src/ServiceProcessorBL2/utils/mem_controller_utils.c:778-783 (ms_write_phy_ram: one PHY RAM window per memory shire); external/core-et/rtl/inc/memshire_defines.vh:40 (DDR_DRAM_DATA_SIZE 16), :48-49 (DDR_NUM_ANIBS 6, DDR_NUM_DBYTES 4); external/et-man/ET Programmer's Reference Manual.pdf pdf p.514 (ddrc_reset_ctl 'DDRC PUB reset')
dram:dram.topo.phy.note: The PHY stores up to four PSTATEs of training values (errata 5.4, pdf p.90) and has a PUB: a Synopsys DesignWare LPDDR4-class PHY, product and version not named in any source. core-et is the Erbium-branch open drop; its memory-shire headers match the ET-SoC-1 firmware wherever both speak (see dram.addr.*).

dram:dram.topo.noc-port.statement: The NoC connects three ports to each memory shire (memory traffic, global-atomic responses, ESR accesses); the memory port is an AXI slave with a 512-bit data path (a whole 64-byte line per beat), and the NoC side delivers at most 32 GB/s per memory shire, almost twice the LPDDR4X side.
dram:dram.topo.noc-port.source: external/et-man/ET Preliminary Datasheet Rev 1.0.pdf pdf p.30 §7.1.1 and §7.1.1.1
