die.name: The ET-SoC-1 die
die.blurb: One slab of silicon about 26 by 22 mm, carrying over 24 billion transistors. It is a grid of 36 tiles called shires (32 compute shires, a master, a spare, a PCIe shire and an I/O shire), eight memory shires down the two sides, and an on-chip network joining them.
die.note: about 25.6-25.8 mm east-west by 22.1-22.2 mm north-south, scaled from Esperanto's die plot to 570 mm2 (chip.die-dims)

shire.name: Compute shire
shire.blurb: A tile of 32 small cores (minions) in four neighbourhoods, with 4 MB of shared on-chip memory, a crossbar joining them, and one stop on the on-chip network. All 34 minion shires are the same design; 32 of them run the programs.
shire.note: one tile pitch: 3.73 mm east-west, 3.70 north-south, measured in pixels on the die plot (chip.hop-pitch)

shire.meshstop.name: Mesh stop
shire.meshstop.blurb: Where the shire joins the on-chip network. Every request that leaves the shire, and every one that comes in, passes through its routers, which pass packets on to the four neighbouring stops.
shire.meshstop.note: order of magnitude only: nine 512-bit routers and their crossings; no floorplan of the shire is published (L114, l2.floorplan)

shire.meshstop.router.name: Router (one of nine main-NoC layers)
shire.meshstop.router.blurb: A small switch. Packets arrive on its input ports, wait in short queues, and an arbiter decides which one crosses the router's internal switch to which output each cycle. Each mesh stop has nine of them stacked as separate networks, plus one for debug.
shire.meshstop.router.note: order of magnitude: an 8-port router with 512-bit datapaths; the NetSpeed configuration is not in the repository

shire.meshstop.router.buf.name: Input buffers (virtual channels)
shire.meshstop.router.buf.blurb: Short queues at each input where packets wait their turn. Each port has four slots (virtual channels), so one blocked packet does not stop the others.
shire.meshstop.router.buf.note: order of magnitude: 8 ports x 4 VC slots of a flit (512 bits or more) each, if flip-flops

shire.meshstop.router.alloc.name: Route computation and allocators
shire.meshstop.router.alloc.blurb: Logic that reads each packet's destination, picks the output (x first, then y, for a request), and arbitrates when two packets want the same output in the same cycle.
shire.meshstop.router.alloc.note: order of magnitude: arbitration logic for 8 ports

shire.meshstop.router.xbar.name: Router switch (crossbar)
shire.meshstop.router.xbar.blurb: A grid of multiplexers that connects any input port to any output port for one cycle. It is wide: a whole 64-byte cache line moves in one beat.
shire.meshstop.router.xbar.note: order of magnitude: an 8 x 8 switch of 512-bit or wider datapaths

shire.meshstop.xing.name: Voltage and clock crossing (VCFIFO)
shire.meshstop.xing.blurb: The shire's cache runs at 0.705 V on its own clock, the network at 0.485 V and 400 MHz. Every bit that crosses is shifted in voltage and re-timed through two flip-flops into the other clock, so it cannot be caught half-changed.
shire.meshstop.xing.note: order of magnitude: a FIFO of a few 512-bit entries with level shifters on every bit

shire.cache.name: Shire cache (four banks)
shire.cache.blurb: The shire's shared 4 MB of fast on-chip memory, in four banks. One memory, three uses: part of it is the shire's cache (L2), part a slice of the chip-wide cache (L3), and part a scratchpad programs manage themselves.
shire.cache.note: order of magnitude: 4 MB of SRAM macros (about 1.1 mm2 of bitcells if HD 6T, more with periphery) and their logic

shire.bank.name: Bank (one of four)
shire.bank.blurb: Each bank is a complete cache of its own, with a queue of waiting requests, a pipeline and four sub-banks of memory. Consecutive 64-byte lines go to banks 0, 1, 2, 3 in turn, so the four work in parallel.
shire.bank.note: order of magnitude: a quarter of the shire cache

shire.bank.reqq.name: Request queue
shire.bank.reqq.blurb: A list of the requests the bank is working on, like a to-do list: 64 entries, each kept from its arrival until its data is back, so many misses can be outstanding at once.
shire.bank.reqq.note: order of magnitude: 64 entries of address and state

shire.bank.rbuf.name: Read buffer
shire.bank.rbuf.blurb: Eight recently read lines kept in registers next to the pipeline. A repeat read is served from here without waking the big memory panels: 36 cycles instead of 47.
shire.bank.rbuf.note: 8 x 512 bits = 4,096 flip-flops at about 1 um2 each (an N7 flip-flop, inference) is about 0.004 mm2, 65 um on a side

shire.bank.dataq.name: Data queue
shire.bank.dataq.blurb: A holding area for the data of requests in flight: one 64-byte line per request-queue entry.
shire.bank.dataq.note: order of magnitude: 64 lines of 576 bits in a two-port register file

shire.bank.atomic.name: Atomic unit
shire.bank.atomic.blurb: A small arithmetic unit beside the memory that performs read-modify-write operations (add, swap, min, max ...) on a word in one place, so that many cores can update a shared counter without racing.

shire.bank.pipe.name: Bank pipeline
shire.bank.pipe.blurb: The assembly line a request moves through, one stage per clock: allocate, arbitrate, read the tags, check them, compare, read the data, check it, send it. Registers between the stages hold each request's state.
shire.bank.pipe.note: order of magnitude: the stage registers and control of one bank

shire.subbank.name: Sub-bank
shire.subbank.blurb: A quarter of a bank: its own tag memory (which lines are here), state memory (valid, dirty, LRU), and four data panels that together hold one 64-byte line per row.
shire.subbank.note: order of magnitude: four data panels of about 150 um plus a tag and a state macro

shire.subbank.tag.name: Tag RAM (1,024 x 116 macro)
shire.subbank.tag.blurb: A small memory that stores, for every set, which four lines (tags) are in it, so a lookup can tell hit from miss.
shire.subbank.tag.note: 118,784 bits at 0.027 um2 is 0.0032 mm2 (57 um square) of cells, more with periphery; if HD 6T (inference)

shire.subbank.state.name: Tag-state RAM (1,024 x 40, two-port)
shire.subbank.state.blurb: A memory read and written on every request: which lines are valid, dirty, locked or all zeros, and the order in which they were used. It has two ports so the read and the update happen in one pass.
shire.subbank.state.note: 40,960 bits; a two-port cell is larger than a 6T cell (order of magnitude)

shire.panel.name: Data panel (4,096 x 144 SRAM macro)
shire.panel.blurb: The basic memory block: a compiled SRAM macro holding 4,096 words of 144 bits (128 data bits and 16 error-check bits). A shire has 64 of them; a line is one row across four panels. Inside: a grid of storage cells, with decoders down one side and sense amplifiers along the bottom.
shire.panel.note: 589,824 bits x 0.027 um2 = 0.016 mm2 of cells; if the array is 1,024 rows x 576 columns of 114 x 237 nm cells it is about 117 x 137 um, some 150 um with its periphery (inference on the unconfirmed m4 reading and the HD cell)

shire.panel.array.name: Bitcell array
shire.panel.array.blurb: The grid of storage cells, each holding one bit: rows are selected by wordlines, and each column's cells share a pair of bitlines that carry the value to the edge.
shire.panel.array.note: 1,024 rows x 114 nm = 117 um tall, 576 columns x 237 nm = 137 um wide, if HD 6T and 4:1 column mux (inference)

shire.panel.decoder.name: Row decoder and wordline drivers
shire.panel.decoder.blurb: Turns the row number into one active wordline: small logic gates decode the address, and a strong driver per row raises that row's wordline across all 576 columns.
shire.panel.decoder.note: a strip the height of the array (inference)

shire.panel.colio.name: Precharge, column mux, sense amplifiers, write drivers
shire.panel.colio.blurb: The circuits along the bottom edge. Before a read they charge every bitline pair high; a tiny difference then appears on the selected pair, and a sense amplifier turns it into a full 0 or 1. For a write, drivers force the bitlines.
shire.panel.colio.note: a strip the width of the array (inference)

shire.panel.ctrl.name: Clock gate and timing control
shire.panel.ctrl.blurb: A clock gate that lets the panel's clock run only for the cycles it is accessed, and the self-timing that decides when the sense amplifiers fire (the trims set its margins).

shire.subbank.ecc.name: ECC (SECDED) logic
shire.subbank.ecc.blurb: Error-correcting code: 8 extra bits stored with every 64 data bits let the logic find and fix any single flipped bit, and detect two. It is trees of exclusive-OR gates.
shire.subbank.ecc.note: order of magnitude: eight 72-bit XOR trees

shire.subbank.cmp.name: Tag comparators
shire.subbank.cmp.blurb: Four comparators check the stored tags against the address at once; the one that matches is the hit way.

shire.l2.name: L2 (a partition of the shire cache)
shire.l2.blurb: The shire's own cache: 512 KB, where a core looks next when its small private cache misses. It is not a separate memory: it is 128 of the 1,024 sets in every sub-bank of the shire cache.
shire.l2.note: spread over all 64 data panels: not a place of its own

shire.l3.name: L3 slice (a partition of the shire cache)
shire.l3.blurb: This shire's 1 MB share of a cache the whole chip shares. It is the top quarter of the rows of the same panels; a line's home slice is chosen by address, so a core usually finds its line in another shire's slice.
shire.l3.note: spread over all 64 data panels: not a place of its own

shire.scp.name: Scratchpad (a partition of the shire cache)
shire.scp.blurb: 2.5 MB of the same panels that programs read and write directly, with no cache in between: never a miss, and any shire can reach it by address.
shire.scp.note: spread over all 64 data panels: not a place of its own

shire.uc.name: UC block
shire.uc.blurb: Hardware for coordination: barrier counters (everyone waits until all have arrived), credit counters, interrupts between cores, and atomic operations that do not go through the cache.
shire.uc.note: order of magnitude: counters, interrupt logic and an atomic ALU

shire.uc.flb.name: Fast local barrier counters
shire.uc.flb.blurb: Thirty-two 8-bit counters. Each thread that reaches a barrier adds one; when the count reaches the number expected, everyone may go on.
shire.uc.flb.note: 32 counters of 8 bits: a few hundred flip-flops

shire.uc.fcc.name: Fast credit counters
shire.uc.fcc.blurb: Per-thread counters that other threads can add credits to; a thread that reads its counter takes a credit, or waits until one arrives. A cheap way to say "your data is ready".
shire.uc.fcc.note: order of magnitude: 4 counters per minion

shire.xbar.name: Crossbar
shire.xbar.blurb: The switch inside the shire that connects each group of eight cores to each of the four memory banks and the UC block. It is wide: 512 bits, a whole cache line, per transfer.
shire.xbar.note: the specification routes the request crossbar "on top of all four banks": it spans the shire cache (l2.xbar.req)

shire.xbar.req.name: Request crossbar
shire.xbar.req.blurb: Carries requests from the 5 clients (4 neighbourhoods and the RBOX) to the 4 banks and the UC block; each bank has a small waiting queue per neighbourhood and a round-robin arbiter.

shire.xbar.rsp.name: Response crossbar
shire.xbar.rsp.blurb: The same switch in reverse: lines coming back from the banks to the neighbourhood that asked.

shire.neigh.name: Neighbourhood
shire.neigh.blurb: Eight minions that share one instruction cache and sit close enough for fast direct links. Esperanto grouped them so because 7 nm wires are slow over longer distances.
shire.neigh.note: if 8 minions of about 0.25 mm2 plus the neighbourhood's logic make about 2.4 mm2, about 1.5 mm on a side (no floorplan published)

shire.neigh.icache.name: Instruction cache (32 KB)
shire.neigh.icache.blurb: Holds the program's instructions for all eight minions. Its tags sit with the minions, but its data memory had to be placed in the shire's higher-voltage region, because those memory cells need the higher voltage.
shire.neigh.icache.note: four 512 x 144 macros of 73,728 bits each; order of magnitude

shire.neigh.l0.name: L0 micro instruction caches (two)
shire.neigh.l0.blurb: Two tiny caches, each serving four minions, that hold the last few instruction lines fetched, so most fetches never reach the 32 KB cache.
shire.neigh.l0.note: 2 x 16 x 512 bits = 16,384 bits of registers: about 0.01 mm2 (order of magnitude)

shire.neigh.req.name: Request path to the banks
shire.neigh.req.blurb: Where the eight minions' requests queue up: arbiters pick one request at a time, and per-bank queues carry them out of the low-voltage region into the shire's high-voltage channel.

shire.neigh.rsp.name: Response path from the banks
shire.neigh.rsp.blurb: Lines coming back cross down to the minions' voltage, wait in a small fill queue, and reach the minion in two 256-bit halves.

shire.neigh.pmu.name: Performance counters (PMU)
shire.neigh.pmu.blurb: Twelve event counters shared by the eight minions' threads.

shire.clock.name: Shire clock generation (PLL, DLL, delay lines)
shire.clock.blurb: Each shire makes its own clock: a phase-locked loop multiplies a reference up to the shire's frequency, and a delay-locked loop feeds the neighbourhoods a copy shifted by half a cycle, corrected for the delay of the wires that carry it.
shire.clock.note: order of magnitude: a digital PLL and a DLL are each on the order of 0.01-0.05 mm2 (inference)

shire.sensors.name: On-die sensors (temperature, process, voltage)
shire.sensors.blurb: Each shire carries a temperature sensor, a process detector and voltage sense points, read by the service processor. The host sees only the average temperature.
shire.sensors.note: order of magnitude: one small analog sensor block

minion.name: Minion
minion.blurb: One of the chip's 1,088 small cores. It runs two threads, has an eight-lane vector unit that also runs the matrix instructions, and a 4 KB data cache, all on one low-voltage supply.
minion.note: if the 32 minions take one half to two thirds of the 13.9 mm2 tile, each is 0.22-0.29 mm2, about 0.5 mm on a side; no floorplan is published (l1.u-floorplan)

minion.hart.name: Hart (hardware thread)
minion.hart.blurb: One of the minion's two threads. Each has its own program counter and registers, and the two take turns issuing instructions into the same pipeline; only thread 0 may issue most of the matrix instructions.
minion.hart.note: a thread is not a place: its registers are spread through the core and the vector unit

core.name: Integer pipeline (the core)
core.blurb: The part that runs ordinary RISC-V instructions one at a time: fetch, decode, read registers, compute, access memory, write back. It also hands vector and matrix work to the vector unit.
core.note: smaller than the vector unit (Esperanto: the vector/tensor unit takes far more area); order of magnitude

core.fe.name: Front end (fetch, thread scheduler, decoder)
core.fe.blurb: Fetches instructions from the shared instruction cache, keeps a small buffer per thread, expands compressed instructions, picks which thread goes next, and decodes.

core.irf.name: Integer register file
core.irf.blurb: The 32 integer registers of each thread: 64 entries of 64 bits, built from latches, with two read ports and one write port.
core.irf.note: 4,096 latch bits at roughly 0.15-0.2 um2 each (an HD latch, inference) is 0.0006-0.0008 mm2: about 25-30 um before the read trees, some 40 um with them

core.alu.name: ALU
core.alu.blurb: The arithmetic-logic unit: adds, subtracts, compares, shifts and does bitwise logic on 64-bit numbers in one cycle.
core.alu.note: order of magnitude: a 64-bit adder, shifter and logic unit

core.muldiv.name: Multiplier and divider
core.muldiv.blurb: An iterative unit: it multiplies 8 bits of the multiplier per cycle (a 64-bit product in 8 cycles) and divides one bit per cycle (65 cycles), so it is small.

core.csr.name: Control and status registers
core.csr.blurb: Special registers that configure the core and start the matrix operations: a tensor instruction is a write to one of these, and runs by itself afterwards.

vpu.name: Vector unit
vpu.blurb: Eight identical lanes that do the same operation on eight numbers at once. Each lane can multiply and add every cycle; the matrix instructions run on these same lanes.
vpu.note: if it takes about half of a 0.25 mm2 minion, about 0.35 mm on a side (order of magnitude)

vpu.lane.name: Lane (one of eight)
vpu.lane.blurb: One lane holds a 32-bit slice of every vector register, a fused multiply-add unit, two 8-bit integer multiply-add units, an integer unit and a unit for exponentials and logarithms.
vpu.lane.note: an eighth of the vector unit (order of magnitude)

vpu.lane.vrf.name: Lane register file (64 x 32 bits, 3 read, 2 write ports)
vpu.lane.vrf.blurb: This lane's 32-bit slice of the 32 vector registers of each thread. Three read ports feed a multiply-add its three operands in one cycle; two write ports take a result and a load together.
vpu.lane.vrf.note: 2,048 bits with five ports: order of magnitude

vpu.lane.fma.name: Fused multiply-add unit (TXFMA)
vpu.lane.fma.blurb: Computes a x b + c on 32-bit floating-point numbers (or two 16-bit ones) in one pass, rounding only once. Inside are a multiplier array, an adder, and circuits that line up and normalise the exponents.
vpu.lane.fma.note: order of magnitude; the multiplier array alone is some 20,000 transistors (see below)

vpu.lane.fma.booth.name: Booth encoders and partial products
vpu.lane.fma.booth.blurb: Multiplication is many shifted additions. Radix-4 Booth encoding looks at the multiplier two bits at a time, halving the number of rows to add: 17 rows for a 32-bit multiplier.

vpu.lane.fma.tree.name: Compressor tree (Wallace tree of 4:2 compressors)
vpu.lane.fma.tree.blurb: The 17 rows are added in a tree of small adders that turn every four bits of a column into two, level after level, until two rows remain for one final adder. This is most of the multiplier's area and most of its switching.

vpu.lane.fma.norm.name: Align, add, normalise, round
vpu.lane.fma.norm.blurb: Floating-point numbers must be lined up by their exponents before adding, and the result shifted back and rounded: a shifter, a wide adder, a leading-zero counter and a rounding adder.

vpu.lane.tima.name: Integer multiply-add units (two TIMA)
vpu.lane.tima.blurb: Two units that multiply 8-bit integers and add the products into 32-bit sums, four at a time each: the int8 matrix work that makes the chip's peak eight times its fp32 rate.

vpu.lane.trans.name: Transcendental unit (exp2, log2, reciprocal)
vpu.lane.trans.blurb: Computes functions like 2^x and log2(x): it looks up three coefficients in small read-only tables and evaluates a quadratic, c0 + c1·m + c2·m², on the lane's own multiply-add unit.

vpu.shsw.name: Shuffle, swizzle and bypass network
vpu.shsw.blurb: Wires and multiplexers that move values between lanes (shuffles), and bypass paths that hand a fresh result to the next instruction before it is written back.

tensor.name: Tensor sequencer
tensor.blurb: Runs the matrix-multiply instructions: state machines that feed the eight lanes step after step for up to 512 cycles from one instruction, with the operands in the L1 scratchpad and a stream buffer.
tensor.note: order of magnitude: state machines and two 1 KiB buffers

tensor.fsm.name: Tensor state machines
tensor.fsm.blurb: Counters and state machines that step through the rows and columns of a matrix tile, injecting one micro-operation into the lanes each cycle.

tensor.tenb.name: TenB (stream buffer for B)
tensor.tenb.blurb: Where the B matrix streams in from the cache on its way to the lanes; the programmer sees 16 registers of 64 bytes, the hardware keeps only what is in flight.

tensor.tenc.name: TenC (int32 accumulators)
tensor.tenc.blurb: Sixteen 64-byte registers that hold the running 32-bit sums of an integer matrix multiply.
tensor.tenc.note: 8,192 bits of register file: order of magnitude

l1d.name: L1 data cache (4 KB)
l1d.blurb: The minion's own small data cache, built from latches rather than SRAM, because it lives on the minion's low voltage. Three quarters of it is set aside as a scratchpad for the matrix instructions.
l1d.note: 32,768 latch bits at roughly 0.15-0.25 um2 each with their read trees is 0.005-0.008 mm2 (70-90 um), plus tags and TLB: order of magnitude

l1d.meta.name: Tags, valid and LRU bits
l1d.meta.blurb: For each of the 64 lines: which address it holds (a 33-bit tag), its state, whether it is valid, and the order of use that picks the next line to replace.
l1d.meta.note: order of magnitude: 2,240 latch bits and 320 flip-flops

l1d.cmp.name: Tag comparators (four)
l1d.cmp.blurb: Four comparators check the four stored tags of a set against the address at once.
l1d.cmp.note: 33 XNORs and an AND tree each: about 10 um (order of magnitude)

l1d.tlb.name: TLB (8 entries)
l1d.tlb.blurb: A tiny table that translates virtual to physical addresses; the documents note virtual memory is unused on this silicon revision.

l1d.mh.name: Miss handlers and replay queue
l1d.mh.blurb: When the cache misses, a miss handler (there are two) fetches the line while the instruction waits in an 8-entry replay queue; the core carries on with other work.

l1d.data.name: Data array (4 LRAM blocks)
l1d.data.blurb: The 4 KB of data: four latch-RAM blocks side by side, each 128 rows of 64 bits; a row across the four blocks is half a cache line.
l1d.data.note: as the L1 minus its tags (order of magnitude)

l1d.block.name: LRAM block (128 x 64)
l1d.block.blurb: One block: a write decoder and a clock gate per row on one side, 128 rows of 64 latches, and a read selector that picks one row onto the 64 output wires.

l1d.row.name: Row and read tree
l1d.row.blurb: One row of 64 latches that all load together when the row's clock gate fires; for reading, each output bit is chosen from 128 rows by a tree of seven levels of two-way switches.
l1d.row.note: 64 latches of about 0.5 um: about 32 um long (inference)

l1scp.name: L1 tensor scratchpad (3 KB)
l1scp.blurb: Three quarters of the L1 cache, set aside before each program to hold a tile of matrix A for the matrix instructions. It is the same latch RAM, used without tags.
l1scp.note: 12 of the L1's 16 sets (order of magnitude)

etlink.name: ET-Link port
etlink.blurb: The minion's doorway to the shire's memory: requests for lines its cache lacks, and evictions, leave here; lines come back in two 256-bit halves.
etlink.note: order of magnitude: interface registers of 256-bit buses

fln.name: Fast local network
fln.blurb: Direct links between some pairs of minions in a neighbourhood, along a tree, for passing register values without going through the caches: 68 cycles round trip, against 114 through the crossbar.
fln.note: its edges join minions a minion-width or two apart: about 0.5 mm (inference)

master.name: Master shire and spare shire
master.blurb: Two more minion shires of the same design. The master runs the chip's own firmware, which starts each program on the compute shires; the spare waits, powered down, to replace a shire lost to a manufacturing defect.

memshire.name: Memory shire
memshire.blurb: One of the eight blocks that connect the chip to its memory chips. Each drives two 16-bit channels through a memory controller per channel and one physical interface (PHY) that sends and receives the signals on the pins.
memshire.note: a cell of the 1.76 mm side strip (L09), and, if the four memory shires of a side sit in the four middle rows as their mesh stops do, one tile pitch tall: about 1.8 x 3.7 mm

memshire.noc.name: NoC port and clock crossing
memshire.noc.blurb: Where requests arrive from the mesh (a whole line per beat) and cross from the network's 400 MHz clock to the memory controller's 933 MHz clock.

memshire.ctrl.name: Memory controllers (two uMCTL2)
memshire.ctrl.blurb: The controllers turn line requests into DRAM commands (open a row, read, write, refresh), reorder them to use open rows, and keep the timing rules of the memory chips.

memshire.phy.name: DDR PHY (one for both channels)
memshire.phy.blurb: The analog front end: drivers that push each bit onto a pin and wire to the memory package, receivers that read the bits coming back, and delay lines that line up the timing.
memshire.phy.note: along the die edge in the 1.76 mm strip; order of magnitude

memshire.phy.dq.name: One DQ pin driver
memshire.phy.dq.blurb: The transistors that drive one data pin: one pulls the line up to the I/O voltage, one pulls it down to ground, sized to drive a trace on the circuit board.
memshire.phy.dq.note: a pin driver's transistors are wide (tens of fins): tens of um (inference)

dram.name: LPDDR4X package (memory chips)
dram.blurb: The card's main memory, off the chip: four packages of 8 GB, each holding four 16-bit channels. Large and cheap, but a load takes about 300 cycles, and a byte costs some 30 times a byte from on-chip memory.
dram.note: the card's part is not identified (dram.org.part); LPDDR4X packages are commonly about 10-15 mm on a side (inference)

dram.chan.name: Channel (one DRAM die or die pair)
dram.chan.blurb: One 16-bit channel: 8 banks, each a large grid of rows; opening a row copies its 16,384 bits into a row of sense amplifiers, from which the 64-byte line is read.
dram.chan.note: a DRAM die is several mm on a side; order of magnitude

dram.bank.name: Bank and subarrays
dram.bank.blurb: A bank is split into many small tiles (mats) of cells between stripes of sense amplifiers and wordline drivers, because long wires would be too slow.

dram.cell.name: DRAM cell and sense amplifier
dram.cell.blurb: A DRAM bit is one transistor and one tiny capacitor: charged is 1, empty is 0. The charge leaks away, so every row is read and rewritten every few tens of milliseconds (refresh).
dram.cell.note: DRAM cells are tens of nm apart, their capacitors far taller; order of magnitude only

pcie.name: PCIe shire
pcie.blurb: The chip's connection to the host computer: two PCIe controllers and an eight-lane physical interface, each lane sending 16 billion bits per second in each direction on a pair of wires.

pcie.ctrl.name: PCIe controllers (two)
pcie.ctrl.blurb: Digital logic that packs reads and writes into PCIe packets, checks them, and retries lost ones.

pcie.phy.name: PCIe PHY (8 lanes)
pcie.phy.blurb: Eight serialiser-deserialiser lanes: each turns parallel data into a 16 GT/s bit stream and back, with a clock recovered from the incoming bits.
pcie.phy.note: along the die edge; order of magnitude

pcie.lane.name: One SerDes lane
pcie.lane.blurb: A transmitter that drives a differential pair of wires, and a receiver that equalises the smeared signal, recovers its clock and decides each bit.

io.name: I/O shire
io.blurb: The chip's housekeeping block: four larger general-purpose cores, the service processor that starts the chip and manages its power and clock speed, the clock generators, the sensor controllers and the peripherals.

io.maxion.name: ET-Maxion cores (four)
io.maxion.blurb: Four out-of-order RISC-V cores for general-purpose control. Unlike a minion, each looks ahead in the program and runs independent instructions early.
io.maxion.note: order of magnitude; out-of-order cores are larger than minions

io.sp.name: Service processor
io.sp.blurb: A single minion core without the vector unit that boots the chip, runs the power and clock governor and answers the host's management commands.
io.sp.note: a minion core without vector unit, plus ROM and 1 MB SRAM (order of magnitude)

io.pll.name: Clock generators (PLL0-PLL4)
io.pll.blurb: Phase-locked loops that multiply the 24 and 100 MHz reference oscillators up to the chip's clocks: the I/O shire's own, the peripherals', the network's 500 MHz (400 on these cards) and the minions' step clock.
io.pll.note: a PLL is on the order of 0.01-0.05 mm2 (inference)

io.pvt.name: PVT controllers (five)
io.pvt.blurb: Controllers that read the temperature sensors, process detectors and voltage monitors spread over the die.

io.periph.name: Peripherals, root of trust, 4 MB cache
io.periph.blurb: USB, I2C, SPI, UART and eMMC interfaces, a hardware root of trust, and another 4 MB of shared cache for the Maxions.

mesh.name: The mesh (network on chip)
mesh.blurb: The on-chip network: a grid of 44 stops, one per shire, joined by links to their neighbours. A message crosses one link per step (a hop); each hop adds 12 cycles to a round trip.
mesh.note: the 6-column shire grid spans about 22.2 mm (L08); with the memory shires the mesh spans the die

mesh.link.name: One hop's link
mesh.link.blurb: The bundle of wires between two neighbouring stops, about 3.7 mm long: hundreds of parallel wires per direction, each broken into segments by repeaters.

mesh.link.wire.name: A wire segment between repeaters
mesh.link.wire.blurb: One wire of the link, from one repeater to the next: a thin copper line whose resistance and capacitance slow the signal, which is why it is re-driven every few hundred micrometres.
mesh.link.wire.note: repeaters every few hundred um (textbook); no ET source gives the spacing

die.power.name: Power delivery (rails, grid, bumps)
die.power.blurb: Power comes in through tens of thousands of solder bumps and spreads over a grid of thick metal. The chip has separate supplies: about 0.52 V for the minions, 0.705 V for the shire caches' memory, 0.485 V for the mesh.

die.clock.name: Clock distribution
die.clock.blurb: A clock is a signal that ticks every cycle at every flip-flop. Each shire makes its own from a shared reference and spreads it through a tree of buffers; clock gates stop it where there is no work.

die.metal.name: The wiring stack (metal layers)
die.metal.blurb: Above the transistors lie a dozen or more layers of copper wires separated by insulator, the lowest ones finest (40 nm pitch), the top ones thick for power and long distances. Vias connect the layers.
die.metal.note: a cross-section of the stack: a few um thick (inference; TSMC does not publish N7's stack heights)

host.name: The host computer
host.blurb: An ordinary desktop PC built on an open frame instead of in a case. The card sits in one of its slots and gets its programs, its data and its power from it.
host.note: An open frame holding an ATX board (30.5 x 24.4 cm) and its power supply: about 45 cm across (estimate from the photo; the frames' make is not recorded).

child.note: the card in the board's first x16 slot (drawn; the slot used on each host is not recorded beyond its root port)

lib.inverter.name: Inverter (NOT gate)
lib.inverter.blurb: The simplest logic gate: one p-type transistor pulls the output up when the input is 0, one n-type pulls it down when the input is 1. Output is always the opposite of the input.
lib.inverter.note: about 2 gate pitches (114 nm) wide in a 240 nm-tall N7 high-density cell (inference from WikiChip Fuse)

lib.nand2.name: NAND gate
lib.nand2.blurb: Output 0 only when both inputs are 1: two p-type transistors in parallel, two n-type in series. Any logic can be built from NAND gates.
lib.nand2.note: about 3 gate pitches wide in a 240 nm cell (inference)

lib.xor.name: XOR / XNOR gate
lib.xor.blurb: Outputs 1 when its inputs differ (XOR) or agree (XNOR): the gate of comparators, adders and error-checking codes.

lib.mux2.name: Two-way multiplexer
lib.mux2.blurb: A switch that passes one of two inputs to the output, chosen by a select signal: trees of them read register files, and grids of them make crossbars.

lib.arbiter.name: Arbiter
lib.arbiter.blurb: Decides who goes next when several requesters want one resource: round-robin arbiters rotate the priority so no one starves.
lib.arbiter.note: order of magnitude: a few dozen gates

lib.fa.name: Full adder
lib.fa.blurb: Adds three bits and gives a sum bit and a carry bit: the brick of every adder and multiplier.

lib.cmp42.name: 4:2 compressor
lib.cmp42.blurb: Takes four bits of a column (and a carry in) and gives two bits out: the step of a multiplier's adder tree that halves the rows at each level.

lib.booth.name: Booth encoder and partial-product selector
lib.booth.blurb: Looks at three overlapping bits of the multiplier and chooses 0, +/-1 or +/-2 times the multiplicand for that row: two multiplier bits per row instead of one.

lib.adder.name: Fast (parallel-prefix) adder
lib.adder.blurb: Adding 64-bit numbers quickly means not waiting for a carry to ripple through 64 positions: prefix adders compute all the carries in about six levels of logic.
lib.adder.note: a 64-bit adder: tens of um (order of magnitude)

lib.latch.name: Latch (the L1's storage cell)
lib.latch.blurb: A bit of memory made of logic: two inverters in a loop hold the value, and a clocked switch lets a new value in while the clock is high. The minion's caches and register files are made of these.
lib.latch.note: about 8-10 gate pitches wide in a 240 nm cell: about 0.1-0.15 um2 (inference)

lib.flipflop.name: Flip-flop (register bit)
lib.flipflop.blurb: Two latches back to back: the value changes only at the clock's rising edge. Pipelines are chains of logic between rows of flip-flops.

lib.icg.name: Clock gate (ICG)
lib.icg.blurb: A latch and an AND gate that stop the clock to a block that has nothing to do, so its flip-flops and clock wires draw no switching power.

lib.levelshift.name: Level shifter
lib.levelshift.blurb: Translates a signal from one supply voltage to another (0.52 V minions to 0.705 V cache, 0.705 V to 0.485 V mesh), so the receiving transistors switch fully.
lib.levelshift.note: order of magnitude: it needs both supplies nearby

lib.sync.name: Synchroniser (two flip-flops)
lib.sync.blurb: Two flip-flops in a row on the receiving clock: a bit that changed just as the clock ticked gets a full cycle to settle before anyone uses it.

lib.senseamp.name: Sense amplifier
lib.senseamp.blurb: A tiny cross-coupled latch that, once fired, amplifies a difference of tens of millivolts between two bitlines into a full 0 or 1.

lib.sram6t.name: 6T SRAM cell
lib.sram6t.blurb: The bit of the shire cache: two inverters in a loop hold the bit, and two access transistors connect it to a pair of bitlines when its row's wordline is raised. Six transistors per bit.
lib.sram6t.note: 0.027 um2: 2 gate pitches (114 nm) x about 8 fin pitches (237 nm), if the macros use N7's high-density cell (inference)

lib.sram8t.name: Two-port register-file cell (8T)
lib.sram8t.blurb: A 6T cell with a separate two-transistor read port, so a row can be read and another written in the same cycle.
lib.sram8t.note: larger than the 6T cell (order of magnitude)

lib.dram1t1c.name: DRAM cell (1T1C)
lib.dram1t1c.blurb: One access transistor and one capacitor. The memory chips on the card are made this way, in a DRAM process, not in the logic process of the ET-SoC-1.
lib.dram1t1c.note: order of magnitude (a DRAM process, not TSMC N7)

lib.wire.name: Copper wiring, in section
lib.wire.blurb: The chip's finest wires are copper, about 20 nm wide and 40 nm apart, wrapped in a thin cobalt liner so that copper atoms do not wander; cobalt contacts take them down to the transistors.
lib.wire.note: the minimum metal pitch of TSMC N7, 40 nm: the finest wires are about 20 nm wide

lib.repeater.name: Repeater
lib.repeater.blurb: A pair of strong inverters placed along a long wire to re-drive the signal, so that the delay grows with the length instead of its square.
lib.repeater.note: a pair of wide inverters (order of magnitude)

lib.clocktree.name: Clock tree
lib.clocktree.blurb: A tree of buffers that brings the clock from the PLL to every flip-flop at nearly the same instant; a delay-locked loop corrects the delay of the branch that feeds the neighbourhoods.
lib.clocktree.note: a shire's clock tree spans its tile

lib.finfet.name: FinFET transistor
lib.finfet.blurb: The switch everything is made of. A voltage on the gate decides whether current flows: at 0 V the path along the fin is shut; at the supply rail (0.517 V on a minion) the gate's field pulls a thin sheet of electrons into the fin, and current flows from source to drain. The gate drapes over the fins on three sides.
lib.finfet.note: one contacted gate pitch of TSMC N7: 57 nm

lib.gate.name: Gate stack
lib.gate.blurb: The gate: a metal electrode on an insulating layer only a few atoms thick (hafnium oxide on a thin silicon oxide), wrapped over the top and both sides of the fin. Its metal's work function sets the voltage at which the transistor turns on.
lib.gate.note: effective gate length about 16.5 nm (N7, Dick James on IEDM 2016); the earlier 20 nm (IRDS, 7 nm-class) is superseded

lib.fin.name: The fin, in section
lib.fin.blurb: A wall of crystalline silicon 6 nm thick and 52 nm tall, tapered with a rounded top; fins stand 30 nm apart. The gate wraps over three sides, so it holds the channel shut tightly: that is why fins replaced flat transistors.
lib.fin.note: N7's fin: 6 nm wide and 52 nm tall (WikiChip Fuse on TSMC's IEDM 2016 paper); the earlier drawing's 6-7 by 45-50 nm, inferred from 10 nm-class sections, is superseded

lib.channel.name: Channel (the silicon under the gate)
lib.channel.blurb: The strip of fin under the gate, 16.5 nm long, where the current flows: about 257,000 silicon atoms and almost no dopant atoms. Off, it is nearly empty of free electrons; on, the gate pulls in about a hundred.
lib.channel.note: the channel's length, the effective gate length of N7: 16.5 nm; the channel is 6 nm wide and 52 nm tall

lib.si.name: Silicon crystal
lib.si.blurb: Silicon atoms in a diamond lattice, each bonded to four neighbours. Every outer electron is held in a bond; freeing one takes 1.12 eV, 43 times the thermal energy at room temperature, so pure silicon barely conducts. A transistor's electrons come from its doped source instead.
lib.si.note: one cubic unit cell: 0.543 nm (NIST CODATA)

fma.tree.col.name: One column of the compressor tree
fma.tree.col.blurb: One bit position of the multiplier: its 17 partial-product bits pass down through layers of 4:2 compressors. Each passes a carry to the next column and takes one from the column before, so the whole tree works in parallel.
fma.tree.col.note: order of magnitude: one bit-column of a tree some 40 um wide

package.name: The package
package.blurb: The chip itself is a thin slab of silicon about 2.6 cm across, mounted face down under this metal lid. The package fans its tens of thousands of microscopic connections out to 2,494 solder balls, big enough to solder onto the card.

child.note: the die, centred under the 45 mm body (assumed)

card.name: The PCIe card
card.blurb: A circuit board about 17 by 11 cm that plugs into the computer. Around the chip sit four memory chips holding its 32 GB, and the regulators that turn the computer's 12 volts into the half a volt its cores run on.
card.note: 6.6 x 4.4 in (167.6 x 111.8 mm), the dev card's assembly drawing (p. 3).
notes: Which heatsink the lab cards carry, and whether each has a fan, is not recorded; the vendor photo shows the card bare.

img.note: The vendor's photo of a dev card (SK hynix DRAM, no heatsink), not a lab card; transparent background. The photo's lid measures 44.8 mm at this scale, which checks the 6.6 in width.

rack.name: The rack
rack.blurb: A wire shelving rack holding about ten open-frame machines on two shelves. The lab's three machines, with their four ET cards, are among them; which ones is not recorded.
rack.note: About 1.5 m wide: five open frames side by side on each shelf (estimate from the photo; common wire-shelving widths are 48-72 in). The rack's make and size are not recorded.
notes: In the page's copy of the photo the machines' tape labels are blurred: they carry host names and network addresses, which the repository keeps out of public pages.

studio45.name: Studio 45
studio45.blurb: Studio 45, a co-working space and workshop for people who build hardware: the lab's rack is here. Light crosses the building in 123 ns, 74 ticks of the chip's clock.
studio45.note: the building at its address, about 37 m deep and 9 m wide (DataSF building footprints); where the rack stands in it is not recorded
notes: No public page ties AI Foundry's lab to Studio 45; the page gives only the name and the city, never an address or a position on the map.

child.note: the rack, drawn to scale; its place in the room is not recorded

sf.name: San Francisco
sf.blurb: The city is about 11 km across. A signal in an optical fibre crosses it in about 54 µs; in that time the chip's clock ticks some 32,000 times.
sf.note: √(121.51 km² of land) = 11.0 km; the city's outline, islands included, spans 16.4 x 17.2 km on the Census map.

child.note: drawn as a small square at the city's centre, labelled "Studio 45 (not to scale; position not shown)"

bayarea.name: The Bay Area
bayarea.blurb: Nine counties around San Francisco Bay, about 200 km from end to end. A fibre signal takes about a millisecond to cross them: some 640,000 of the chip's clock ticks.
bayarea.note: The nine counties span 204 x 219 km on the Census outlines.

california.name: California
california.blurb: The state is about 1,000 km from north to south. A fibre signal runs its length in about five thousandths of a second.
california.note: 908 x 1060 km on the equal-area map (Census 1:5,000,000).

us.name: The United States
us.blurb: From coast to coast about 4,500 km. A signal in a fibre from San Francisco to New York takes about 20 ms one way even on a perfectly straight cable: 12 million clock ticks of the chip.
us.note: The longest great circle inside the lower 48 states: 2,802 mi (4,509 km), Florida to Washington.

earth.name: Earth
earth.blurb: Earth is 12,742 km across. Light could circle it in 134 ms: in that time the chip's clock ticks 80 million times.
earth.note: Mean diameter 12,742 km (twice NASA's volumetric mean radius, 6,371.000 km).

img.credit: NASA Goddard Space Flight Center, "The Blue Marble" (Visible Earth record 57723, globe_west): image by Reto Stöckli; enhancements by Robert Simmon; MODIS data
img.licence: public domain (NASA imagery is generally not subject to copyright in the US; NASA asks to be credited as the source)
img.note: North America centred; the disc fills about 88% of the square (measure it in the page).

moon.name: Earth and the Moon
moon.blurb: The Moon is 384,400 km away. Light takes 1.28 s to get there: 770 million ticks of the chip's clock.
moon.note: The Moon's orbit: semimajor axis 384,400 km, so about 769,000 km across.

solar.name: The Solar System
solar.blurb: Sunlight takes 8.3 min to reach Earth and about 4.2 h to reach Neptune. In November 2026 Voyager 1, the farthest spacecraft, will be a full light-day away.
solar.note: Neptune's orbit: semimajor axis 30.07 au (4,498 million km), so about 9.0 x 10^12 m across.

child.note: Earth's position on its 1 au orbit (for the zoom, the angle is arbitrary)

stars.name: The nearest stars
stars.blurb: The nearest star after the Sun, Proxima Centauri, is 4.2 light-years away: its light left it more than four years ago.
stars.note: A 20-light-year frame around the Sun (a choice, not an object).

milkyway.name: The Milky Way
milkyway.blurb: Our galaxy: at least 100 billion stars in a disc about 100,000 light-years across. The ET-SoC-1 has about a quarter as many transistors as the galaxy has stars.

img.credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech/R. Hurt (SSC/Caltech), "Our Milky Way Gets a Makeover" (artist's concept, PIA10748)
img.licence: JPL image use policy: "may be used for any purpose without prior permission"; credit "NASA/JPL-Caltech"

geometry.how: same artwork and framing as ESO's annotated eso1339e (correlation 0.977 at scale 1.0, no shift); its distance rings, centred on the Sun, are 9.45 px per 1,000 ly on the 1280 px screen image; the Sun is marked at (640, 884) of 1280.

img.note: An artist's concept, not a photograph: nobody has seen the galaxy from outside. Say so on the page.

localgroup.name: The Local Group (Andromeda)
localgroup.blurb: The Milky Way's neighbourhood: dozens of galaxies (more than 130 are now known, most of them faint dwarfs), led by the Milky Way and Andromeda. The light we see from Andromeda left it 2.5 million years ago. There is no "Andromeda cluster": Andromeda is a galaxy, and it and the Milky Way lead this small group. True clusters, such as Virgo with over a thousand galaxies, are larger, and lie further out inside Laniakea.
localgroup.note: Its galaxies are spread over a diameter of nearly 10 million light-years (NASA).

child.note: the Milky Way on the map

img.licence: JPL image use policy: "may be used for any purpose without prior permission"; credit "NASA/JPL-Caltech"
img.note: An ultraviolet mosaic, so bluer than to the eye; no scale bar on the photo (its framing in light-years is not given).

laniakea.name: Laniakea
laniakea.blurb: The Local Group is one small part of a supercluster of about 100,000 galaxies, about 520 million light-years across. Its name is Hawaiian for "immeasurable heaven".
laniakea.note: 160 Mpc across if taken as round (Tully et al. 2014): 522 million light-years.

universe.name: The observable universe
universe.blurb: Everything whose light has had time to reach us since the Big Bang, 13.8 billion years ago: a sphere about 92 billion light-years across, larger than 13.8 billion because space has stretched while the light travelled.
universe.note: Twice the comoving distance to the particle horizon: 14.16 Gpc = 46.2 billion ly radius, from Planck 2018's parameters (H0 67.66, Ωm 0.3111, ΩΛ 0.6889, radiation from T = 2.7255 K, Neff 3.046).

child.note: a dot at the centre (Laniakea is ~1/180 of the diameter)

img.credit: NASA / WMAP Science Team, "Nine Year Microwave Sky" (WMAP 2012)
img.note: A map of the whole sky (Mollweide projection): the inside of the sphere, not a view from outside. Transparent outside the ellipse.

beyond.name: Beyond what we can see (speculative)
beyond.blurb: Space almost certainly goes on past the edge of what we can see, but how far is unknown. Some theories go further and propose many universes, a multiverse: a hypothesis, not an observation. (This level is the page's reading of the owner's "meta universe".)
beyond.note: Unknown. The frame is only a picture size.

lib.dramcell.name: A DRAM cell, in section
lib.dramcell.blurb: A DRAM bit is charge on one tiny capacitor, reached through one transistor. With no circuit to restore it, the charge leaks away, so every row is read and rewritten every 32 ms. Drawn generically: the card's DRAM is made on a DRAM process, not TSMC N7, and its generation is not known.

p.atom.name: A silicon atom
p.atom.blurb: One of the crystal's atoms: a tiny nucleus with 14 electrons around it. Only the outer four take part in bonds and in electronics; the other ten sit deep inside, held 20 to 300 times more tightly.

p.dopant.name: A dopant atom: phosphorus in the crystal
p.dopant.blurb: A foreign atom in a silicon atom's place. Phosphorus brings five outer electrons, one more than the bonds need, and that spare electron is free to carry current; boron brings three, leaving a gap (a hole) that carries current the other way. This is how a transistor's source and drain are made to conduct.

p.nucleus.name: The silicon-28 nucleus
p.nucleus.blurb: Fourteen protons and fourteen neutrons, packed together by the strong force: a thirty-thousandth of the atom's width but 99.97% of its mass. Nothing in a chip ever touches it.

p.nucleon.name: A proton
p.nucleon.blurb: A proton is three quarks (up, up, down) held by gluons; a neutron is up, down, down. Unlike the electron, it has a real size, because it is a bound state, and most of its mass is the energy of what goes on inside.

p.quark.name: A quark
p.quark.blurb: As far as any experiment can tell, a quark is a point. The disc here is only the limit: if a quark has a size, it is smaller than this, under a two-thousandth of the proton. Quarks are never found alone; pull one out and the energy makes new quarks.

bound.words: no size measured: a radius under 4.3 × 10⁻¹⁹ m

p.electron.name: An electron
p.electron.blurb: The particle that carries every current in the chip. Its charge and mass are known to 10 digits, but no experiment has found any size: as far as we know it is a point. The 'cloud' of the atom is where the electron is likely to be, not the electron itself.

bound.words: no size measured: a radius under 2 × 10⁻²⁰ m

p.planck.name: The Planck length
p.planck.blurb: The length built from gravity, quantum mechanics and the speed of light. Here, physicists expect space and time themselves to need a quantum description that nobody has yet; whether anything can be smaller is unknown. Between the quark's limit and here lie 16 powers of ten that no experiment has reached.

p.wrap.name: The ring of sizes
p.wrap.blurb: This is not further out in space. The ring is a picture of every size at once, the smallest joined to the largest; the links across it are physics, not distance. Looking far out is looking back in time, to an early universe that was a sea of quarks.

bernal.name: Bernal Heights
bernal.blurb: Bernal Heights, a hill neighbourhood of about 26,000 people in south-east San Francisco. The hill is red chert: quartz, silicon dioxide, from the shells of plankton that lived 100 to 200 million years ago. Refined, the same silicon is the die. Light crosses the neighbourhood in 7.3 µs, about 4,400 of the chip's clock ticks.

st29.name: 29th Street
st29.blurb: 29th Street, 1.3 km long, drops about 95 m from the hills of Noe Valley to the flats where the Mission meets Bernal Heights. Light runs its length in 4.3 µs, about 2,600 ticks of the chip's clock.

lib.nor2.name: NOR gate
lib.nor2.blurb: Out is 1 only when both inputs are 0: two p-type transistors in series pull it up, two n-type side by side pull it down. With the NAND, any logic can be built from it.

lib.aoi21.name: AND-OR-INVERT gate
lib.aoi21.blurb: One stage of transistors that computes not (A·B + C): cheaper and faster than an AND, an OR and an inverter. A fast adder's carry cells are made of these.

lib.shifter.name: Shifter (stages of multiplexers)
lib.shifter.blurb: Moves a number left or right by any number of places in a few steps: each stage shifts by 1, 2, 4, ... places or not. The multiply-add uses one to line up the numbers it adds and another to normalise the result.

lib.lzd.name: A leading-zero counter
lib.lzd.blurb: Counts the zeros before the first 1 of a number, in a tree of small cells: it tells the normaliser how far to shift a sum so that its first digit is a 1.

lib.decoder.name: Decoder
lib.decoder.blurb: Turns an address into one raised line: 3 bits pick one of 8 rows, 7 bits one of 128. Every memory and register file has one for its rows.

lib.regfile.name: Register file
lib.regfile.blurb: A small, fast memory with several doors: rows of latches, a decoder that picks the row to write, and multiplexers that read one row out per port. Processors keep their registers in these.

lib.logic.name: Control logic: standard cells
lib.logic.blurb: What any block of control logic is made of when its own netlist is not published: flip-flops that hold its state and a few kinds of gate that compute the next state, all from a library of standard cells.

lib.counter.name: Counter
lib.counter.blurb: A register that adds one to itself on every clock (or every event): flip-flops and a chain of half adders. Barrier counters, credit counters and performance counters are all of this kind.

lib.cmpeq.name: Equality comparator
lib.cmpeq.blurb: Says whether two numbers are equal: an XNOR gate per bit, then a tree of gates that is 1 only if every bit agreed. A cache uses one per way to find its hit.

lib.fifo.name: Queue (first in, first out)
lib.fifo.blurb: Where requests wait their turn: a small register file, a counter that points where the next one is written, another where the next one is read, and a compare that says full or empty.

lib.pll.name: A phase-locked loop (PLL)
lib.pll.blurb: Makes a fast clock from a slow, steady one: it compares the two, and nudges an oscillator (a ring of inverters) until its output, divided down, matches the reference.

lib.ecc.name: Error correction (SECDED)
lib.ecc.blurb: Extra check bits stored with the data, each the parity of some of the bits: on a read they show whether a bit flipped, which one, so it can be put right, and whether two did.

lib.rom.name: A read-only memory (ROM)
lib.rom.blurb: A table fixed when the chip is made: a transistor where a bit is 0, none where it is 1. The vector unit's transcendental functions read their coefficients from small tables like this.

lib.diffamp.name: A differential amplifier
lib.diffamp.blurb: Two matched transistors that share one current: the higher input takes more of it. It amplifies the difference between two wires and ignores what they share, which is how a receiver hears a weak signal through noise.

lib.xbar.name: A crossbar switch
lib.xbar.blurb: Connects any input to any output for one cycle: a multiplexer per output picks the input its arbiter chose. In the chip it is 512 bits wide, so it is mostly wires.

lib.round.name: Rounding
lib.round.blurb: The exact product and sum are longer than a float can keep: three extra bits say whether the kept part rounds up by one at its last place, to the nearest value, a tie to the even one.

lib.buck.name: A buck converter (a switching regulator)
lib.buck.blurb: How 12 volts becomes half a volt without burning the rest as heat: two transistors connect an inductor to 12 V or to ground, hundreds of thousands of times a second, and the inductor and a capacitor smooth the pulses into a steady supply.

lib.powerfet.name: A power transistor, in section
lib.powerfet.blurb: A switch for tens of amps: thousands of small transistor cells side by side, each passing current straight down through the silicon from its source on top to the drain underneath.

lib.strap.name: A boot switch and its pin
lib.strap.blurb: A switch on the card holds one of the chip's pins at 0 or lets a resistor pull it to 1; when the chip comes out of reset it reads the pin and starts accordingly.

p.cu.name: A copper atom
p.cu.blurb: Copper: 29 electrons around a nucleus of 29 protons. In the metal each atom gives its one outer electron to a shared sea that flows when a voltage pushes it: that is the current in every wire of the chip.
